children.title: Search-Tree Representation Calculus
children.top_down_role: Representations and partition choices that generate the search tree before traversal, propagation, and learning policies are selected.

knowledge_statements.title: Labeling Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain CSP search tree whose edges label variable-value decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=(X,D,C)\) be a finite-domain constraint satisfaction problem. A labeling tree for \(P\) is a rooted tree whose root carries the empty assignment and whose node \(v\) carries a consistent partial assignment \(\alpha_v\). If an internal node selects an unassigned variable \(x\), its outgoing edges have labels \(x=a\) for distinct \(a\in D(x)\), and the child reached by \(x=a\) carries \(\alpha_v\cup\{x=a\}\). The selected edge labels must cover every value of \(x\) compatible with \(\alpha_v\). A leaf is successful when its assignment satisfies every constraint and failed when it has no satisfying extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A labeling tree recursively assigns values to variables; exhaustive outgoing labels preserve all possible solutions, and leaves represent solutions or dead ends.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and every domain \(D(x)\) are finite.
Every tree node has a unique root-to-node path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every root-to-leaf path denotes one partial or complete assignment generated by successive labeling decisions.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-domain constraint-programming search-tree definition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition, notation, plain-text summary, and content kind fit the Labeling Trees container. No inspectable citation or source locator is supplied, so source support is required before candidate review acceptance.

assumptions_latex: Each branch constraint is interpreted over the variables of its parent residual problem.
Every internal node has finitely many children.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every branching step is exhaustive, then \(\operatorname{Sol}(P_0)\) is covered by the solution sets of the terminal residual problems.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard residual-subproblem representation of exhaustive search
termination hypothesis added for terminal-leaf coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search tree represented by the subproblem remaining after each branch decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an initial finite-domain constraint problem \(P_0\), a residual-problem tree is a rooted tree in which each node \(v\) is labeled by a residual problem \(P_v\). The root label is \(P_0\). If the outgoing branch constraints at \(v\) are \(B_{v,1},\ldots,B_{v,k}\), then child \(i\) is labeled by \(P_{v,i}=P_v\wedge B_{v,i}\). The branches are exhaustive when \(\operatorname{Sol}(P_v)=\bigcup_i\operatorname{Sol}(P_{v,i})\), and nonduplicating when these solution sets are pairwise disjoint. A node is terminal if its residual problem is inconsistent, solved, or accepted by the specified search stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each node stores the problem left after its path decisions. Exhaustive children cover the parent's solutions, disjoint children avoid duplication, and termination of every search path ensures that terminal residual problems cover the initial solution set.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Problem Trees

assumptions_latex: \(P_0\) is a finite-domain constraint problem.
\(F\) is sound, contracting, and terminates on every generated residual problem.
The generated tree is finite, or every maximal search path terminates at a leaf.
Every consistent terminal residual problem contributes all of its represented solutions to the search output.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If branching is exhaustive, the solution sets output at the consistent terminal leaves cover \(\operatorname{Sol}(P_0)\).

notation.meaning: propagation-reduced residual problem at node v

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard sound-propagation reduction of a finite-domain search tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-problem tree normalized by sound propagation at every generated node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a sound, contracting propagation operator on finite-domain residual problems. A propagation-reduced tree has root label \(F(P_0)\). If node \(v\) has label \(Q_v\) and branch constraint \(B_{v,i}\), its child candidate is \(F(Q_v\wedge B_{v,i})\); the child is discarded or marked failed when propagation detects inconsistency. Soundness means \(\operatorname{Sol}(F(Q))=\operatorname{Sol}(Q)\), while contraction means that every propagated domain is contained in its input domain. Thus propagation may remove values and inconsistent subtrees but cannot remove a solution represented by an exhaustive branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagation is applied after every branch, shrinking residual domains and eliminating detected failures without changing the represented solution set. When every search path terminates and consistent terminal residual problems output all represented solutions, exhaustive branching remains complete.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation-Reduced Trees

children.title: Enumeration Trees
children.top_down_role: Tree structures used to traverse feasible assignments or solutions without objective-driven pruning.

knowledge_statements.title: Enumeration Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete, nonduplicating search tree for enumerating every feasible assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite constraint problem \(P\), an enumeration tree is a finite residual-problem tree whose branching is exhaustive and nonduplicating at every internal node. Every successful leaf determines exactly one member of \(\operatorname{Sol}(P)\), and every member of \(\operatorname{Sol}(P)\) reaches a successful leaf. Failed leaves have empty solution sets. Consequently, the successful leaves are in bijection with \(\operatorname{Sol}(P)\). If propagation is used, it must preserve solution sets; if a leaf retains multiple solutions, a terminal enumeration operation must output each of them exactly once.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An enumeration tree exhaustively partitions the feasible set so that every solution is produced exactly once and failed leaves produce none.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) has finitely many feasible assignments.
Every internal branching family is exhaustive and pairwise solution-disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The outputs of all successful leaves form \(\operatorname{Sol}(P)\) without omission or duplication.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard exhaustive and nonduplicating enumeration-tree specification
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly characterizes complete, nonduplicating enumeration and fits the Enumeration Trees leaf. Its caveat for terminal leaves containing multiple solutions is consistent with output-level enumeration. No inspectable citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Optimization Trees
children.top_down_role: Tree structures shaped by incumbent bounds, objective comparisons, or optimization-specific pruning.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search tree augmented with objective bounds and incumbent-based pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite minimization problem with objective \(f\). An optimization tree is an exhaustive residual-problem tree in which each live node \(v\) has a valid lower bound \(L_v\leq\min\{f(x):x\in\operatorname{Sol}(P_v)\}\), with the minimum interpreted as \(+\infty\) for an infeasible node. The incumbent value \(U\) is the least objective value of any solution found so far. A node may be pruned when it is infeasible or when \(L_v\geq U\). Search terminates when no live node remains; a stored incumbent attaining \(U\) is then optimal, unless no incumbent exists, in which case \(P\) is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimization tree combines exhaustive branching with valid node bounds and prunes nodes that cannot improve the best solution found.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}(P)\) is finite.
Every node bound is valid and all unpruned branching steps are exhaustive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, the incumbent is globally optimal, or absence of an incumbent certifies infeasibility.

notation.meaning: valid lower bound at node v

children.title: Feasibility-to-Optimization Tree Transitions
children.top_down_role: Structural changes that arise when an enumeration search acquires an optimization objective.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) has a finite feasible set and \(f:\operatorname{Sol}(P)\to\mathbb{R}\) is minimized.
Branching is exhaustive, propagation is sound, and branching makes sufficient progress to produce a finite search tree.
For every live node \(v\), the bound satisfies \(L_v\leq\min\{f(x):x\in\operatorname{Sol}(P_v)\}\), with the minimum interpreted as \(+\infty\) when \(P_v\) is infeasible.
Every live node is eventually selected unless it is pruned by infeasibility or by its valid bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs a global minimizer of \(f\) over \(\operatorname{Sol}(P)\), or correctly reports that \(P\) is infeasible.

notation.meaning: valid lower bound at node v

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard transition from feasibility enumeration to branch-and-bound optimization
incumbent discovery no longer closes an incompletely searched node
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of exhaustive feasibility search into incumbent-and-bound optimization search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite feasible-set model \(P\), an objective \(f\) to minimize, an exhaustive feasibility branching rule, and a valid node-bound oracle. Initialize the incumbent value \(U:=+\infty\), store no incumbent solution, and place the root residual problem in the live set. Repeatedly select a live node \(v\), apply sound propagation, and discard the node if propagation proves it infeasible. Compute a valid lower bound \(L_v\) and discard the node if \(L_v\geq U\). Any feasible solution \(x\) found while processing the node updates the incumbent when \(f(x)<U\), but finding such a solution does not by itself close a residual problem that may contain better solutions. If the residual problem is completely solved, evaluate all solutions it outputs and close the node; otherwise generate exhaustive children and add them to the live set. Stop when the live set is empty and output the stored incumbent, or report infeasibility if no incumbent exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add an objective, valid lower bounds, and incumbent updates to exhaustive feasibility search. A newly found solution improves the incumbent but does not close a node that may contain a better solution; the node must instead be solved, exhaustively branched, or safely pruned.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-to-Optimization Tree Transitions
Value-Enumeration Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiway branching that assigns one selected variable to each remaining value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a residual finite-domain problem \(P_v\), select a variable \(x\) with current domain \(D_v(x)=\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}\), where \(k\geq2\). Value-enumeration branching creates children \(P_{v,i}=P_v\wedge(x=a_i)\) for \(i=1,
\ldots,k\), followed optionally by sound propagation. The branch predicates are mutually exclusive and exhaustive over \(D_v(x)\), so \(\operatorname{Sol}(P_v)=\mathbin{\dot\bigcup}_{i=1}^k\operatorname{Sol}(P_{v,i})\). Children detected inconsistent may be removed without changing this union.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a variable and create one child for each current value; the children partition the parent’s solutions by that variable’s value.
assumptions_latex: \(P_v\) is a finite-domain residual problem.
The selected domain contains at least two distinct values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated children form an exhaustive, pairwise disjoint solution partition of the parent node.

notation.meaning: current domain of variable x at node v

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment–Exclusion Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary branching between assigning a selected value and excluding it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At residual problem \(P_v\), choose a variable \(x\) and a value \(a\in D_v(x)\). Assignment–exclusion branching creates the two children \(P_v^+=P_v\wedge(x=a)\) and \(P_v^-=P_v\wedge(x\neq a)\), equivalently replacing the domain of \(x\) by \(\{a\}\) and by \(D_v(x)\setminus\{a\}\), respectively. The two branch predicates are complementary; hence their solution sets are disjoint and their union equals \(\operatorname{Sol}(P_v)\). Either child may subsequently be reduced by sound propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch into assigning a chosen value and excluding that value; the two children are complementary and partition all parent solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(P_v\) is a finite-domain residual problem.
\(a\in D_v(x)\) and \(|D_v(x)|\geq2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}(P_v)=\operatorname{Sol}(P_v^+)\mathbin{\dot\cup}\operatorname{Sol}(P_v^-)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard assign-or-exclude binary branching rule

children.title: Interval Splitting
children.top_down_role: Branches formed by subdividing ordered numeric domains into interval regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary partition of an ordered integer domain at a threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the current finite integer domain of \(x\) be \(D_v(x)\subseteq\mathbb Z\), and choose an integer threshold \(t\) satisfying \(\min D_v(x)\leq t<\max D_v(x)\). Interval splitting creates children with branch constraints \(x\leq t\) and \(x\geq t+1\). Their induced domains are \(D^- =D_v(x)\cap(-\infty,t]\) and \(D^+=D_v(x)\cap[t+1,\infty)\). Both are nonempty, disjoint, and satisfy \(D_v(x)=D^-\mathbin{\dot\cup}D^+\); therefore the children partition the parent’s solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split an ordered integer domain at a threshold into lower and upper parts, producing two exhaustive and disjoint children.
assumptions_latex: \(D_v(x)\) is a finite subset of \(\mathbb Z\) with at least two elements.
The threshold lies between the domain minimum and maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraints \(x\leq t\) and \(x\geq t+1\) define a binary partition of the current domain and solution set.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The threshold conditions make both integer subdomains nonempty and give an exhaustive disjoint partition, so the definition fits Interval Splitting. No supporting citation or locator is present.

children.title: Set Splitting
children.top_down_role: Branches formed by partitioning finite collections of candidate values or elements.

knowledge_statements.title: Set Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branching by a disjoint partition of an arbitrary finite domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) have current finite domain \(D_v(x)\), and choose nonempty sets \(S_1,\ldots,S_k\) with \(k\geq2\) such that \(D_v(x)=\mathbin{\dot\bigcup}_{i=1}^k S_i\). Set splitting creates child \(i\) by adjoining the membership constraint \(x\in S_i\), equivalently restricting the domain of \(x\) to \(S_i\). The resulting child solution sets are pairwise disjoint and their union is \(\operatorname{Sol}(P_v)\). Sound propagation may further reduce each child without invalidating this partition at the level of solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition a finite domain into nonempty subsets and create one membership branch per subset, thereby partitioning the parent’s solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(P_v\) is a finite-domain residual problem.
The sets \(S_i\) are nonempty, pairwise disjoint, and cover \(D_v(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}(P_v)=\mathbin{\dot\bigcup}_{i=1}^k\operatorname{Sol}(P_v\wedge(x\in S_i))\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-set partition branching rule
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-set partition and membership branches correctly induce an exhaustive, nonduplicating solution partition. The content kind fits Set Splitting, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Split Balance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Balanced, skewed, or adaptive partition shapes for interval-based or set-based branching.

knowledge_statements.title: Split Balance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative classification of domain partitions by their largest child block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a partition \(D=\mathbin{\dot\bigcup}_{i=1}^k S_i\) of a finite domain with \(|D|\geq2\), define its imbalance ratio by \(\rho=\max_i|S_i|/|D|\). For a prescribed \(\beta\in[1/k,1)\), the split is \(\beta\)-balanced when \(\rho\leq\beta\), and \(\beta\)-unbalanced when \(\rho>\beta\). A perfectly size-balanced split satisfies \(\max_i|S_i|-\min_i|S_i|\leq1\). Along a path using \(\beta\)-balanced splits, the selected domain size after \(h\) successive splits is at most \(\beta^h|D|\), up to integer rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balance is measured by the largest child’s fraction of the parent domain; uniformly balanced splitting yields geometric domain shrinkage along paths.
assumptions_latex: Every block \(S_i\) is nonempty.
The same bound \(\beta<1\) applies at each split considered along the path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After \(h\) balanced splits, every descendant block has size at most \(\lceil\beta^h|D|\rceil\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary finite-partition balance measure and geometric shrinkage consequence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The imbalance ratio, balance threshold, perfect size-balance condition, and geometric descendant-size bound are internally consistent for repeated splits of descendant blocks. Because the named balance regimes and terminology are not backed by any cited source, authoritative terminology support with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Constraint Branching
children.top_down_role: Branches expressed through added constraints over the residual problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branching by adjoining an exhaustive family of alternative constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a residual constraint problem \(P_v\), constraint branching selects constraints \(B_1,\ldots,B_k\) and creates children \(P_{v,i}=P_v\wedge B_i\). The family is valid for exhaustive search when every solution of \(P_v\) satisfies at least one \(B_i\), equivalently \(P_v\models B_1\vee\cdots\vee B_k\). It is partitioning when additionally \(P_v\models\neg(B_i\wedge B_j)\) for all \(i\neq j\). Valid branching preserves completeness; partitioning branching also prevents a parent solution from appearing in multiple children. Sound propagation may be applied after each constraint is adjoined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Create children by adding alternative constraints whose disjunction covers the parent; pairwise incompatibility additionally makes the branches nonduplicating.
assumptions_latex: \(P_v\) is a residual constraint problem.
The selected family \(B_1,\ldots,B_k\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exhaustiveness gives \(\operatorname{Sol}(P_v)=\bigcup_i\operatorname{Sol}(P_v\wedge B_i)\), with a disjoint union under partitioning.

notation.meaning: residual child formed by adjoining B_i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard exhaustive constraint-disjunction branching semantics
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The entailment conditions correctly distinguish exhaustive constraint branching from pairwise-disjoint partitioning branching, and definition is the appropriate content kind. No authoritative constraint-programming citation or specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Disjunction Branching
children.top_down_role: Branches organized as explicit alternatives within a covering disjunction.

assumptions_latex: The current search state has feasible completion set \(F\subseteq\Omega\).
The branch predicates \(B_1,\ldots,B_m\) are decidable and satisfy \(F\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^m B_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The children preserve every feasible completion: \(F=\bigcup_{i=1}^m(F\cap B_i)\).

notation.meaning: Feasible completions compatible with the current search state.
Predicate set defining child branch i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite, exhaustive disjunction branching at one search node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given the current feasible completion set \(F\), choose finitely many decidable branch predicates \(B_1,\ldots,B_m\) whose union covers \(F\). Create child \(i\) by adjoining predicate \(B_i\) to the current constraint store, propagate that store, and discard the child if propagation detects inconsistency. Search each surviving child according to the selected traversal rule. The branching step is exhaustive because \[F=F\cap\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^m B_i\right)=\bigcup_{i=1}^m(F\cap B_i).\] Overlap among the \(B_i\) is permitted unless unique assignment of completions to children is separately required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Create one child per predicate in an exhaustive finite disjunction, propagate each child, discard inconsistent children, and search all survivors.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjunction Branching

children.title: Constraint-to-Disjunction Encodings
children.top_down_role: Correspondences and structural tradeoffs between constrained branches and disjunctive branch families.

assumptions_latex: The current constraint store is \(C\), with feasible set \(F(C)\).
The candidate branch constraints \(c_1,\ldots,c_m\) are interpreted over the same ambient assignment space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraint family is an exact disjunctive encoding precisely when \(F(C)=\bigcup_{i=1}^m F(C\wedge c_i)\).

notation.meaning: Feasible assignments satisfying a constraint store.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasible-set encoding of constraint branches as a disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite family of branch constraints \(c_1,\ldots,c_m\) is an exact constraint-to-disjunction encoding at store \(C\) when \[C\models c_1\lor\cdots\lor c_m,\qquad F(C)=\bigcup_{i=1}^m F(C\wedge c_i).\] It is a disjoint encoding when additionally \(F(C\wedge c_i\wedge c_j)=\varnothing\) for all distinct \(i,j\). Thus replacing the parent by children with stores \(C\wedge c_i\) preserves the parent feasible set; disjointness further gives every feasible assignment a unique child.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch constraints encode a disjunction exactly when their child feasible sets cover the parent feasible set; pairwise inconsistency makes the encoding disjoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-to-Disjunction Encodings

children.title: Set-Variable Branching
children.top_down_role: Branch partitions over membership, inclusion, exclusion, or set-bound decisions.

assumptions_latex: A set variable \(S\) has finite lower and upper bounds \(L\subseteq S\subseteq U\).
An undecided element \(e\in U\setminus L\) is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The children \(e\in S\) and \(e\notin S\) form a disjoint exhaustive partition of the current set domain.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary include-exclude branching for finite bounded set variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite set variable with domain \(\mathcal D(S)=\{T:L\subseteq T\subseteq U\}\), choose \(e\in U\setminus L\). Create an inclusion child with bounds \(L\cup\{e\}\subseteq S\subseteq U\) and an exclusion child with bounds \(L\subseteq S\subseteq U\setminus\{e\}\), then propagate each child. Their domains are disjoint and satisfy \[\mathcal D(S)=\{T\in\mathcal D(S):e\in T\}\mathbin{\dot\cup}\{T\in\mathcal D(S):e\notin T\}.\] Stop branching on \(S\) when \(L=U\); the unique remaining value is then \(S=L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an undecided element and branch on including or excluding it; the two propagated children disjointly exhaust the bounded set domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Variable Branching

children.title: Sequence-Variable Branching
children.top_down_role: Branch partitions over ordering, predecessor, successor, or placement decisions.

assumptions_latex: The sequence variable \(Q\) ranges over a finite set \(D\) of admissible finite sequences.
The selected position \(k\) exists in every sequence \(q\in D\), and at least two distinct values occur at position \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(V_k=\{q_k:q\in D\}\), the children imposing \(Q_k=v\), indexed by \(v\in V_k\), form a disjoint exhaustive partition of \(D\).

notation.meaning: Selected position, defined in every sequence in the current domain.
Values occurring at the selected position.
Child domain associated with value v.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Position-value branching for finite sequence domains in which the selected position exists in every current sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\) be a position that exists in every sequence \(q\in D\) and is not fixed throughout \(D\). Define \(V_k=\{q_k:q\in D\}\). For every \(v\in V_k\), create a child imposing \(Q_k=v\), propagate all sequence constraints, and let its resulting domain be \(D_v=\{q\in D:q_k=v\}\). Before propagation-based deletion of infeasible values, the child domains satisfy \[D=\mathbin{\dot\bigcup}_{v\in V_k}D_v.\] Empty children may be discarded. The rule can be reapplied at any position that remains unfixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a position present in every current sequence and create one propagated child for each value occurring there; the children disjointly cover the current sequence domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequence-Variable Branching

children.title: Scheduling-Variable Branching
children.top_down_role: Branch partitions over temporal, resource, precedence, or activity-placement decisions.

assumptions_latex: A scheduling state has feasible schedules \(F\), and two activities \(i,j\) cannot overlap in any schedule under consideration.
Each activity \(a\) has start time \(s_a\) and duration \(p_a\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The precedence children \(s_i+p_i\leq s_j\) and \(s_j+p_j\leq s_i\) cover \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary precedence branching for a selected nonoverlapping activity pair.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.5 Set Covering with Many Variables: Crew Scheduling p. 57

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose activities \(i,j\) whose relative order is unresolved and whose simultaneous execution is forbidden. Create one child imposing \(s_i+p_i\leq s_j\) and another imposing \(s_j+p_j\leq s_i\); propagate temporal and resource constraints in both children. For every feasible nonoverlapping schedule, at least one precedence holds, so \[F=(F\cap\{s_i+p_i\leq s_j\})\cup(F\cap\{s_j+p_j\leq s_i\}).\] The children may intersect only in zero-slack boundary schedules where both precedence inequalities hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two activities that cannot overlap, branch on their two possible precedence orders and propagate temporal and resource constraints in each child.
knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling-Variable Branching

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4.5 Set Covering with Many Variables: Crew Scheduling p. 57

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The precedence disjunction is mathematically plausible, and the algorithm role fits the leaf. However, the cited locator concerns a set-covering crew-scheduling formulation and does not inspectably support precedence branching on a nonoverlapping activity pair. A direct scheduling or constraint-programming source is required.

children.title: Cross-Domain Branch Coordination
children.top_down_role: Coordination of branching choices when set, sequence, or scheduling objects coexist.

assumptions_latex: The search state has variables from domains \(X_1,\ldots,X_r\) and current feasible completion set \(F\).
Each available branching family is finite and exhaustive for the state where it is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Adaptive selection among domain-specific exhaustive families preserves global coverage of \(F\).

notation.meaning: Branch predicates selected at state u.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage-preserving adaptive coordination of heterogeneous branch families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each nonterminal state \(u\), a coordinator may select a branch family from any represented domain type using propagation scores or another deterministic rule. If the selected predicates satisfy \(F_u\subseteq\bigcup_i B_{u,i}\), then the child sets \(F_{u,i}=F_u\cap B_{u,i}\) preserve coverage regardless of which domain supplied the predicates. Hence cross-domain selection is complete provided every selected local family is exhaustive and the search traversal eventually processes every surviving child; coordination changes search order and partition shape, not the set of reachable feasible completions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinator may switch among heterogeneous branching families without losing solutions when every selected family is exhaustive and every surviving child is eventually processed.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Domain Branch Coordination

assumptions_latex: A search node has feasible completion set \(F\subseteq\Omega\).
A finite family \(\mathcal B=(B_i)_{i=1}^m\) defines its children.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family covers the node exactly when \(F\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^m B_i\), equivalently \(F=\bigcup_{i=1}^m(F\cap B_i)\).

notation.meaning: Finite family of branch predicate sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local coverage criterion for a finite branch family.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite branch family \(\mathcal B=(B_i)_{i=1}^m\) is a coverage family for the current node when every feasible completion belongs to at least one branch predicate: \[F\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^m B_i.\] Equivalently, its child feasible sets satisfy \(F=\bigcup_{i=1}^m(F\cap B_i)\). A coverage certificate consists of the predicates together with a valid implication from the current constraint store to \(B_1\lor\cdots\lor B_m\). Coverage alone does not require disjoint children or strict domain reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite branch family covers a node when every feasible completion satisfies at least one branch predicate; overlap and strict reduction are separate properties.
knowledge_statements.title: Branch-Coverage Families

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

children.title: Disjoint Partitions
children.top_down_role: Branch families whose alternatives occupy nonoverlapping portions of the current search region.

assumptions_latex: The family \((B_i)_{i=1}^m\) covers the current feasible completion set \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: It is a disjoint partition exactly when \(F\cap B_i\cap B_j=\varnothing\) for all \(i\neq j\).

notation.meaning: Child feasible set for branch i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise-disjoint finite partition of a node's feasible completions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A covering branch family \((B_i)_{i=1}^m\) induces a disjoint partition of \(F\) precisely when \[F\cap B_i\cap B_j=\varnothing\qquad\text{for every }i\neq j.\] With \(F_i=F\cap B_i\), coverage and pairwise disjointness jointly give \(F=\mathbin{\dot\bigcup}_{i=1}^m F_i\). Consequently, every feasible completion has exactly one child containing it. Empty children may be deleted without changing either coverage or disjointness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A covering branch family is a disjoint partition when no feasible completion belongs to two different children; each completion then has a unique child.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjoint Partitions

children.title: Overlapping Partitions
children.top_down_role: Branch families whose alternatives may revisit shared portions of the current search region.

assumptions_latex: The family \((B_i)_{i=1}^m\) covers the current feasible completion set \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: It is overlapping exactly when \(F\cap B_i\cap B_j\neq\varnothing\) for some \(i\neq j\).

notation.meaning: Child feasible set for branch i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite covering families whose feasible child sets intersect.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A covering family \((B_i)_{i=1}^m\) is overlapping on \(F\) when at least one feasible completion belongs to multiple children, equivalently when \[F\cap B_i\cap B_j\neq\varnothing\quad\text{for some }i\neq j.\] Coverage still gives \(F=\bigcup_i(F\cap B_i)\), so no feasible completion is lost. However, a completion in an intersection may be explored through several children unless duplicate detection, canonical ownership, or an equivalent symmetry-breaking rule removes the duplication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A covering family overlaps when some feasible completion occurs in multiple children; coverage remains valid, but duplicate exploration can result.
knowledge_statements.title: Overlapping Partitions

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

children.title: Overlap Multiplicity
children.top_down_role: Sources and degrees of repeated coverage created by overlapping branches.

assumptions_latex: A finite branch family \((B_i)_{i=1}^m\) covers a nonempty feasible completion set \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Its overlap multiplicity is \(\mu=\max_{x\in F}|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:x\in B_i\}|\), with \(1\leq\mu\leq m\).

notation.meaning: Branch membership count of feasible completion x.
Maximum number of children containing one feasible completion.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum pointwise membership count in a finite covering family.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each feasible completion \(x\in F\), define its branch membership count by \(d(x)=|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:x\in B_i\}|\). The overlap multiplicity of the family is \[\mu=\max_{x\in F}d(x)=\max_{x\in F}|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:x\in B_i\}|.\] Coverage implies \(1\leq\mu\leq m\). The family is disjoint on \(F\) exactly when \(\mu=1\); values \(\mu>1\) quantify the largest number of child subproblems that can contain the same feasible completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Overlap multiplicity is the largest number of children containing one feasible completion; for a covering family, it equals one exactly when the children are disjoint on the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Overlap Multiplicity

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

children.title: Partition Conversion Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits and costs of replacing overlapping alternatives with disjoint alternatives.

assumptions_latex: A finite family \((B_i)_{i=1}^m\) covers the feasible set \(F\).
A conversion must use predicates expressible in a fixed branch language \(\mathcal L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A disjoint conversion within \(\mathcal L\) exists by sequential subtraction only if every \(B_i\cap\bigcap_{j<i}B_j^{\mathsf c}\) is representable in \(\mathcal L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representability boundary for disjointizing an overlapping finite cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Any ordered finite cover can be disjointized set-theoretically by \(D_1=B_1\) and \(D_i=B_i\cap\bigcap_{j<i}B_j^{\mathsf c}\) for \(i>1\), yielding \[F\cap\bigcup_{i=1}^m B_i=F\cap\mathbin{\dot\bigcup}_{i=1}^m D_i.\] Conversion fails within a restricted predicate language \(\mathcal L\) when some required complement or intersection is not representable in \(\mathcal L\). Even when representable, the conversion can exceed an imposed branch-count or formula-size budget, so set-theoretic convertibility does not imply admissible or compact convertibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential subtraction disjointizes any finite cover, but conversion can fail operationally when the branch language lacks complements or intersections, or size limits are exceeded.
knowledge_statements.title: Partition Conversion Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, and sequential set-theoretic disjointization is standard. However, the domain-cut locator does not inspectably support the asserted branch-language and formula-budget boundaries. Moreover, failure of syntactic closure under a particular complement or intersection does not by itself exclude an equivalent predicate in the language; the relevant condition must be stated in terms of representability of each disjointized set. A direct source is needed before selecting the exact corrected formulation.

assumptions_latex: Every nonterminal search state \(u\) is assigned a value \(\rho(u)\) in a well-founded ordered set \((W,\prec)\).
Every generated nonempty child \(v\) satisfies \(\rho(v)\prec\rho(u)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No search branch is infinite; with finite branching, the entire search tree is finite.

notation.meaning: Progress rank assigned to a state.
Well-founded strict order on progress values.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Well-founded rank condition certifying finite propagation-guided search.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite progress measure is a map \(\rho\) from search states into a well-founded ordered set \((W,\prec)\) such that every nonempty child \(v\) of a nonterminal state \(u\) satisfies \(\rho(v)\prec\rho(u)\). Well-foundedness excludes an infinite descending chain, so no root-to-leaf search branch can be infinite. If every state has finitely many children, the resulting search tree is finite. For finite domains, a typical rank is the total number of unresolved domain alternatives, provided each branch strictly reduces that number after propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A well-founded rank that strictly decreases in every surviving child rules out infinite branches; finite branching then yields a finite search tree.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Progress Measures

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

children.title: Redundant Branches
children.top_down_role: Branches that add duplicate or logically unnecessary search coverage.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is finite and does not contain \(B\).
\(f\) is defined on every feasible complete assignment when optimization is considered.
The infimum of an empty feasible set is interpreted as \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(B)\subseteq\bigcup_{Q\in\mathcal A}F(Q)\) permits deletion of \(B\) without changing feasibility or the infimum objective value.

notation.meaning: Feasible complete assignments extending branch Q.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports semantic branch redundancy in constraint-programming search.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic redundancy relative to the other active branches of a finite minimization search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\) be an active branch, let \(\mathcal A\) be the finite family of other active branches, and, for each branch \(Q\), let \(F(Q)\) be its set of feasible complete assignments. The branch \(B\) is redundant relative to \(\mathcal A\) when
\[F(B)\subseteq\bigcup_{Q\in\mathcal A}F(Q).\]
Deleting \(B\) then preserves the existence of a feasible assignment. For every objective \(f\) defined on feasible complete assignments, it also preserves the infimum objective value over the union of active branches, with the infimum of the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). This definition concerns feasibility or optimization, not duplicate-free enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branch is redundant when every feasible completion it contains also occurs in the union of the other active branches. Removing it preserves feasibility and the infimum objective value, but need not preserve duplicate-free enumeration.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Branches

children.title: Dominated Branches
children.top_down_role: Branches made structurally inferior by another alternative under the relevant search criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Dominated Branches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solution-mapping dominance for finite minimization search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\) be an active branch, let \(\mathcal A\) contain alternative active branches, and let \(f\) be minimized. The branch \(B\) is dominated by \(\mathcal A\) if there exists a map
\[\phi:F(B)\longrightarrow\bigcup_{Q\in\mathcal A}F(Q)\]
such that \(f(\phi(x))\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in F(B)\). Thus every feasible completion of \(B\) has an alternative completion that is no worse. Unlike redundancy, dominance need not require the same assignments to occur in the alternative branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branch is dominated when each of its feasible completions can be replaced by a feasible completion in another branch with no worse objective.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a minimization objective on all feasible complete assignments.
\(\phi\) is defined for every element of \(F(B)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{Q\in\mathcal A,\,x\in F(Q)}f(x)\leq\min_{x\in F(B)}f(x)\) whenever \(F(B)\neq\varnothing\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports solution-mapping dominance between CP search branches.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The solution-mapping definition is mathematically coherent and fits the definition leaf, but no citation or inspectable locator supports this specific notion of dominance between CP search branches.

children.title: Redundancy Detection Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where redundant coverage is difficult or costly to recognize.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundancy Detection Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of deciding semantic redundancy from sound but incomplete propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Semantic redundancy is a set-inclusion property and need not be detected by sound propagation. Let \(x,y\in\{0,1\}\), impose \(x=y\), and consider branches \(B_x=(x=0)\) and \(B_y=(y=0)\). Then
\[F(B_x)=F(B_y)=\{(0,0)\}.\]
Nevertheless, the sound identity propagator, which performs no domain reduction, leaves the restricted domain vectors of the two branches unequal and does not certify their equivalence. Hence soundness of propagation alone cannot make failure to detect redundancy evidence that redundancy is absent; completeness requires stronger reasoning about the represented constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Redundancy is semantic. A sound but incomplete propagator may miss two branches with identical feasible completions, so nondetection does not establish nonredundancy.
assumptions_latex: The propagator is required to be sound but not complete for logical consequence.
Branch redundancy is interpreted through feasible-completion sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(B_x)=F(B_y)\) can hold even though propagation does not certify either branch as redundant.

notation.meaning: Branches fixing x or y to zero.

review_flags: Concrete boundary is self-contained, but no supplied source directly covers incomplete propagation and branch-redundancy detection.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is internally valid and the failure_boundary kind fits the leaf, but the record supplies no source for the claimed boundary between sound propagation and semantic redundancy detection.

children.title: Dominance-Safe Pruning
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions governing removal of dominated branch alternatives.

assumptions_latex: The retained branches remain available for search.
The dominance map preserves feasibility and never worsens the minimized objective.
The infimum of an empty feasible set is interpreted as \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in U_{\mathcal A}}f(x)=\inf_{x\in F(B)\cup U_{\mathcal A}}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Union of the feasible-completion sets of the retained branches.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports dominance-safe pruning in CP search.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition for pruning a dominated branch in minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\) be a branch proposed for pruning, let \(\mathcal A\) be the retained family of active branches, and define
\[U_{\mathcal A}=\bigcup_{Q\in\mathcal A}F(Q).\]
Suppose the active frontier represents \(F(B)\cup U_{\mathcal A}\). If there is a map \(\phi:F(B)\to U_{\mathcal A}\) such that \(f(\phi(x))\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in F(B)\), then
\[\inf_{x\in U_{\mathcal A}}f(x)=\inf_{x\in F(B)\cup U_{\mathcal A}}f(x),\]
where the infimum of the empty set is \(+\infty\). The equality also holds when \(F(B)=\varnothing\). Thus removing \(B\) preserves the best attainable minimization value, but it need not preserve every feasible or every optimal assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branch may be pruned without changing the best minimization value when every one of its feasible completions maps to a retained feasible completion with no worse objective. Such pruning need not preserve all feasible or optimal assignments.
knowledge_statements.title: Dominance-Safe Pruning

children.title: Complete Propagation-Based Search
children.top_down_role: Systematic traversal families and the levels of constraint reasoning maintained between decisions.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Sections 4.3 and 4.8, Constraint Propagation and Best-First Search

children.title: Candidate Generation
children.top_down_role: Organization of candidate production before complete constraint validation.

knowledge_statements.title: Candidate Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Child generation at a propagated finite-domain search state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a nonfailed propagated state \(S\) with an unassigned variable. Select a variable \(x\) with current finite domain \(D_S(x)\), and choose a finite family of restrictions \(R_1,\ldots,R_k\) satisfying
\[\operatorname{Sol}(S)=\bigcup_{i=1}^k\operatorname{Sol}(S\wedge R_i).\]
Generate candidate children \(S_i=S\wedge R_i\), optionally ordering them by a search heuristic. Submit each child to propagation and testing. If no variable is unassigned, emit \(S\) as a complete candidate rather than branching. Completeness requires retaining every nonfailed child unless a sound pruning rule removes it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an unassigned variable and generate finitely many child restrictions whose feasible completions cover those of the parent; then send each child for testing.
assumptions_latex: Every current variable domain is finite.
The branching restrictions cover every solution of the parent state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}(S)=\bigcup_{i=1}^k\operatorname{Sol}(S_i)\), so exhaustive processing of unpruned children is complete.

notation.meaning: Current domain of x in S.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports finite-domain CP candidate generation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The covering child-generation procedure fits the algorithm leaf and is internally precise, but no source or locator is supplied for finite-domain CP candidate generation or its completeness condition.

children.title: Candidate Testing
children.top_down_role: Validation regimes applied to generated complete or partial candidates.

knowledge_statements.title: Candidate Testing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound testing of generated partial or complete candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a generated state \(S\), apply a sound propagator to a fixpoint, obtaining \(P(S)\). If propagation reports failure, reject \(S\). If \(P(S)\) is complete, evaluate every original constraint and accept exactly when all are satisfied; for optimization, also record its objective value. Otherwise retain \(P(S)\) for further branching. A nonfailed incomplete state is not thereby certified feasible: sound incomplete propagation may leave a state having no feasible completion. Thus testing has three outcomes—reject, accept complete solution, or continue search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagate each candidate; reject detected failure, validate complete assignments against all constraints, and continue branching on incomplete nonfailed states.
assumptions_latex: Propagation removes no feasible completion.
Complete assignments can be checked against every original constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A rejected state has no feasible completion, while an accepted state is a feasible complete assignment.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the three-outcome CP candidate-testing cycle.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three-outcome testing procedure is mathematically consistent and appropriately classified as an algorithm, but it has no supporting citation or inspectable locator.

children.title: Generation–Testing Granularity
children.top_down_role: Placement of validation relative to the amount of candidate structure already generated.

knowledge_statements.title: Generation–Testing Granularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Number of branching decisions made between successive tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a generation–testing search cycle, its granularity \(g\) is the maximum number of new branching restrictions conjoined along a candidate path after one test and before the next. Fine-grained search has \(g=1\): every generated child is propagated and tested immediately. If \(g>1\), up to \(g\) restrictions may be accumulated before testing. Full-assignment generate-and-test has \(g\) equal to the remaining decision depth. Completeness is unchanged when branching remains covering and final testing is exact, but larger \(g\) can postpone detection of inconsistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Granularity counts how many branching decisions may be generated between tests; larger granularity preserves completeness under exact final testing but can delay rejection.
assumptions_latex: Branching restrictions cover all feasible completions.
Every complete generated assignment eventually receives an exact test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Increasing \(g\) changes rejection timing, not completeness under covering generation and exact terminal testing.

notation.meaning: Maximum decisions accumulated between consecutive tests.

review_flags: No supplied locator defines generation–testing granularity for propagation-guided search.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed granularity parameter is coherent and fits a definition leaf, but it appears to be a specialized formalization and no source defines it or supports the associated completeness claim.

children.title: Late-Rejection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Search behavior when infeasibility is exposed only after substantial candidate construction.

knowledge_statements.title: Late-Rejection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential leaf rejection when testing is deferred until assignments are complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(n\) Boolean variables and the constraint
\[x_1\oplus x_2\oplus\cdots\oplus x_n=0.\]
A generate-and-test procedure that branches over all Boolean assignments and tests this constraint only after all \(n\) variables are fixed generates \(2^n\) complete candidates and rejects exactly \(2^{n-1}\) of them at depth \(n\). Thus exhaustive completeness does not prevent exponentially many late rejections. Earlier parity propagation or incremental testing can detect the required value of the final variable once the preceding values are fixed, avoiding generation of the inconsistent final child.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deferred testing of an even-parity constraint generates all Boolean assignments and rejects half only at depth n, exhibiting exponentially many late failures.
assumptions_latex: Candidates are tested against parity only after all \(n\) variables are assigned.
Both Boolean values are generated at every depth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure generates \(2^n\) leaves and rejects \(2^{n-1}\) leaves only at depth \(n\).
review_flags: The counting example is explicit, but no supplied source addresses late rejection in generate-and-test CP search.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parity count is correct and the failure_boundary kind matches the late-rejection leaf, but the record provides no citation for its use as a CP generation-testing boundary or for the propagation comparison.

knowledge_statements.title: Chronological Backtracking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Depth-first finite-domain search returning to the most recent open decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the current state to the root and maintain an ordered sequence of decision frames. At a nonfailed incomplete state, generate a covering ordered list of children, record its untried alternatives, and descend into the first child after propagation. On failure, or after processing a solution when enumeration continues, restore the state preceding the most recent frame having an untried child and descend into that child. Delete exhausted frames in reverse creation order. Stop when a requested solution is found or no frame has an untried child; in the latter case the finite search tree is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Depth-first search returns after failure to the newest decision with an untried alternative, exhausting decisions in last-in, first-out order.
assumptions_latex: The generated search tree is finite.
Every branching family covers the feasible completions of its parent.
Propagation and pruning are sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exhaustion without a solution certifies infeasibility; otherwise every reported assignment satisfies the original constraints.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports chronological backtracking for finite-domain CP.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm accurately describes chronological depth-first backtracking under the stated finite-tree, coverage, and soundness assumptions, but no authoritative source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Recursive Realizations
children.top_down_role: Search implementations whose traversal state follows recursive call structure.

assumptions_latex: The recursion depth and every branching factor are finite.
Generated children cover their parent's feasible completions.
Propagation and complete-assignment validation are sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{DFS}(S)\) returns a feasible completion when one is found and failure only after all covered descendants are exhausted.

notation.meaning: Recursive search invoked on state S.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the recursive realization of propagation-guided backtracking.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive depth-first realization of chronological backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\operatorname{DFS}(S)\) recursively. First propagate \(S\); return failure if propagation fails. If the resulting state is complete, validate and return or emit it. Otherwise generate an ordered covering family \(S_1,\ldots,S_k\). For \(i=1,\ldots,k\), call \(\operatorname{DFS}(S_i)\); return immediately if the search convention requests only the first solution, and otherwise continue through all children. Return failure after every child fails. The programming-language call stack stores parent states, the next child index, and return points, thereby realizing chronological depth-first backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursive depth-first search propagates a state, handles failure or completion, and recursively explores each covering child while the call stack stores control state.
knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Realizations

children.title: Iterative Realizations
children.top_down_role: Search implementations whose traversal state is represented by explicit iterative control structures.

assumptions_latex: The generated search tree is finite.
Children are generated in a fixed order.
Propagation and pruning are sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterative procedure exhausts exactly the same ordered search tree as the corresponding recursive depth-first procedure.
review_flags: The supplied iterative-method locator does not specifically support iterative CP backtracking.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit-stack realization of chronological depth-first backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a last-in, first-out stack with the root state. Repeatedly pop its top state \(S\), propagate it, and discard it on failure. If the propagated state is complete, validate and emit it. Otherwise generate ordered children \(S_1,\ldots,S_k\) and push them in reverse order, \(S_k,\ldots,S_1\), so that \(S_1\) is processed next. Stop upon the first solution when requested, or when the stack is empty. With identical propagation, child ordering, and pruning, this procedure visits states in the same depth-first order as the recursive realization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An iterative depth-first search uses a LIFO stack, pushing children in reverse desired order to reproduce recursive chronological backtracking.
knowledge_statements.title: Iterative Realizations

children.title: Explicit Search-State Storage
children.top_down_role: Storage choices for pending branches, restoration points, and traversal context.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Search-State Storage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frame-and-trail representation for restorable depth-first search states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Represent each open decision by a frame
\[\mathcal F=(r,j,\mathcal R,m),\]
where \(r\) identifies the branching variable or decision, \(j\) is the next untried alternative, \(\mathcal R\) is the ordered alternative list, and \(m\) is a restoration marker into a reversible trail. The trail stores every domain or constraint-state modification needed to undo propagation. Before trying an alternative, restore the trail to \(m\), apply that alternative, and propagate. The storage invariant requires restoration to reproduce exactly the parent state represented when the frame was created.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each explicit frame stores a decision, remaining alternatives, and a trail marker; restoring to the marker must exactly reconstruct the parent state.
assumptions_latex: Every mutable search-state update is reversible or copied.
A frame remains stored while it has an untried alternative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Restoring to \(m\) reconstructs the frame's parent state before the next alternative is applied.

notation.meaning: Ordered alternatives belonging to the frame.
Restoration marker in the reversible trail.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports frame-and-trail state storage for CP search.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The frame-and-trail invariant fits the representation leaf and is internally consistent, but no source or specific locator supports this CP search-state representation.

children.title: Control-Stack Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Depth, memory, interruption, or resumability limits associated with control-state organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Control-Stack Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness boundary for recursive or iterative depth-first CP implementations using mutable decision-local and global search state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the mutable search state into decision-local state \(L\) and global state \(G\), and let \(m\) be the checkpoint immediately before a branch decision. After that branch fails, restoration must satisfy \(\operatorname{restore}(L,m)=L_{\mathrm{parent}}\). Information retained in \(G\) may survive only when it is valid for every remaining sibling. If a decision-local domain deletion, constraint activation, local objective restriction, or propagator datum created below \(m\) survives restoration without such validity, a feasible sibling may be removed and search may become incomplete. If restoration revives decision-local information invalidated at or above \(m\), search may admit an infeasible leaf. Stack unwinding is therefore correct only when decision-local effects are persistent or completely trailed and every untrailed global effect is valid for the remaining search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backtracking must restore all decision-local state to the parent checkpoint. Global information may persist only when it remains valid for every sibling; otherwise leaked or over-restored mutations can lose solutions or admit infeasible leaves.
assumptions_latex: The search tree is finite and branching is exhaustive.
Propagation and every globally retained inference are sound for the remaining search.
Mutable effects are classified as decision-local or globally valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Correct sibling exploration requires \(\operatorname{restore}(L,m)=L_{\mathrm{parent}}\), while retained global state must remain valid for every sibling.

notation.meaning: Globally retained search information valid beyond one branch.
Trail or restoration checkpoint for a decision level.

knowledge_statements.title: Backtracking with Consistency Checking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chronological finite-domain backtracking that tests constraints after extending a partial assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite CSP \(P=(X,D,C)\), initialize the partial assignment \(A=\varnothing\). At a node, if every variable is assigned, output \(A\). Otherwise choose an unassigned variable \(x\), and for each \(a\in D(x)\), form \(A'=A\cup\{x=a\}\). Recurse on \(A'\) exactly when every constraint whose scope is fully assigned by \(A'\) is satisfied; otherwise reject that branch. If every value fails, return failure to the parent and undo \(x\)'s assignment. Exhaustive value enumeration with chronological restoration returns a solution if one exists and failure otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign one variable at a time, reject an extension when a fully instantiated constraint fails, and chronologically backtrack after exhausting the selected variable's values.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and every domain \(D(x)\) are finite.
Every constraint can be evaluated on a complete assignment to its scope.
Variable and value selection eventually enumerate every child.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a satisfying assignment exactly when the finite CSP is satisfiable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and finite-CSP completeness claim fit the container and are mathematically standard, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward Checking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step lookahead for binary finite-domain CSP search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a binary finite CSP, extend the current assignment by \(x=a\). For every unassigned neighbor \(y\) of \(x\), replace its current domain by \[D'(y)=\{b\in D(y):(a,b)\in R_{xy}\}.\] Leave domains of nonneighbors unchanged. Reject the branch if some \(D'(y)=\varnothing\); otherwise continue search using the reduced domains. On backtracking, restore all deletions made at this decision level. Forward checking examines only constraints joining the newly assigned variable to an unassigned variable and does not enforce consistency between two unassigned variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After assigning a variable, delete incompatible values from each unassigned neighbor; fail on an empty domain and restore all deletions during backtracking.
assumptions_latex: The CSP is finite and its relevant constraints are binary relations.
The current partial assignment is consistent.
Every domain deletion is reversible on backtracking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every deleted value is incompatible with the new assignment, and an empty neighbor domain soundly certifies branch failure.

notation.meaning: Binary compatibility relation between variables x and y.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary forward-checking algorithm is precise and locally appropriate, but the record has no citation with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Lookahead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restricted propagation between forward checking and full maintained arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a deterministic subset selector \(Q(A,x,a)\) of directed constraint arcs. After extending partial assignment \(A\) by \(x=a\), initialize a worklist with \(Q(A,x,a)\). Repeatedly revise only an arc \((u,v)\) removed from this worklist, deleting each \(b\in D(u)\) having no compatible support in \(D(v)\); enqueue only additional arcs permitted by \(Q\). Reject the branch upon an empty domain, and otherwise branch from the resulting state. Restore all deletions on backtracking. The method is sound but need not reach the full arc-consistency closure unless \(Q\) schedules every arc affected by every deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial lookahead propagates along a prescribed subset of affected arcs; its deletions are sound, but its fixpoint can be weaker than full arc consistency.
assumptions_latex: The CSP is finite and binary.
Arc revision deletes only values lacking compatible support.
The selected worklist policy is deterministic and finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reduced domains preserve every solution extending \(A\cup\{x=a\}\), though they may not be arc consistent.

notation.meaning: Policy selecting arcs processed after the decision.
Directed binary-constraint arc revised from u toward v.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: “Partial lookahead” has multiple established variants, and the proposed arbitrary selector policy Q is not shown to match the intended local variant. A source defining this exact scheduling policy is needed.

knowledge_statements.title: Maintaining Arc Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: MAC for binary finite-domain CSPs after every search decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At the root, and after every decision \(x=a\), place every directed arc affected by a domain change into a worklist. For an arc \((u,v)\), delete \(b\in D(u)\) whenever no \(c\in D(v)\) satisfies the binary relation \(R_{uv}\). Whenever \(D(u)\) shrinks, enqueue the other arcs whose supports may thereby be lost. Continue until the worklist is empty or a domain becomes empty. Branch only from a nonempty arc-consistent closure; reject an empty-domain node and restore the preceding closure when backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MAC restores the arc-consistency closure after each decision, rejects empty-domain nodes, and restores the previous domains when backtracking.
assumptions_latex: The CSP is finite and binary.
Arc revision is sound and is scheduled until a fixpoint.
Domain changes are restored correctly on backtracking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each surviving search node is arc consistent, and no solution extending that node is removed.

notation.meaning: Compatibility relation on a binary constraint.
Directed arc whose first domain is revised.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated binary MAC procedure and conclusion are standard and fit the algorithm container, but no authoritative citation or locator is provided.

children.title: Maintaining Generalized Consistency
children.top_down_role: Lookahead search maintaining generalized consistency over nonbinary or global constraint scopes.

knowledge_statements.title: Maintaining Generalized Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maintaining generalized arc consistency for finite-domain constraints of arbitrary arity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite CSP with constraints \(c\), after each decision initialize a worklist with every pair \((c,x)\) affected by a changed domain, where \(x\in\operatorname{scope}(c)\). Delete \(a\in D(x)\) if there is no tuple \(t\in c\) satisfying \(t_x=a\) and \(t_y\in D(y)\) for every other scoped variable \(y\). Each deletion schedules all affected constraint-variable pairs. Stop at the generalized-arc-consistency fixpoint, reject an empty domain, and restore deletions on backtracking. Branch only from a nonempty fixpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After every decision, repeatedly remove values lacking a supporting tuple in each incident constraint until generalized arc consistency or an empty domain is reached.
assumptions_latex: All variables and domains are finite.
Each constraint supplies an exact support test.
Every affected constraint-variable pair is eventually processed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At a surviving node, every \(a\in D(x)\) has a current support in every constraint containing \(x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maintained-GAC procedure is mathematically coherent and fits the container, but its support criterion and maintained-fixpoint claim lack an inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Maintaining Stronger Consistency
children.top_down_role: Lookahead search maintaining consistency levels stronger than the baseline generalized regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Maintaining Stronger Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search maintaining a chosen consistency property stronger than generalized arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a sound, contracting, idempotent consistency operator on finite-domain search states, and suppose its fixpoint implies generalized arc consistency. Compute \(K(S_0)\) at the root. After each branching restriction producing state \(S\), compute \(K(S)\); reject the node if \(K(S)\) contains an empty domain or an explicit contradiction, otherwise branch from \(K(S)\). On backtracking restore the parent's fixpoint. If every deletion made by \(K\) removes no solution represented by \(S\), exhaustive branching remains complete while potentially detecting failures earlier than generalized arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply a sound consistency closure stronger than GAC after every decision; reject contradictions and branch from the closure while restoring parent states on backtracking.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) terminates on every finite search state.
\(K\) preserves exactly all solutions represented by its input state.
Branching is exhaustive over the surviving state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maintaining \(K\) preserves search soundness and completeness and yields nodes at least as filtered as GAC.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The abstract closure formulation is plausible, but “stronger consistency” does not identify a unique consistency family. A source is needed to establish the intended operator class and its relation to GAC.

children.title: Consistency-Strength Escalation
children.top_down_role: Transitions between maintained consistency levels as search conditions change.

knowledge_statements.title: Consistency-Strength Escalation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance relation between sound propagation closures used at the same search node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) be sound closure operators on the same finite-domain states. Say that \(K_2\) is at least as strong as \(K_1\) when \(K_2(S)\preceq K_1(S)\) for every state \(S\), where \(S'\preceq S\) means every domain and represented relation in \(S'\) is contained in its counterpart in \(S\). Escalating from \(K_1\) to \(K_2\) cannot retain a value deleted by \(K_1\) and cannot remove a solution, but it does not guarantee a smaller total runtime because computing \(K_2\) may cost more.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stronger sound closure produces a state contained in that of a weaker closure, preserving solutions but not necessarily improving total runtime.
assumptions_latex: Both operators act on the same state representation.
Both closures are sound and terminate.
Strength is compared pointwise on every admissible state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_2(S)\preceq K_1(S)\) gives propagation dominance, not runtime dominance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise containment definition correctly separates filtering dominance from runtime dominance and fits a principle container, but no supporting citation is supplied.

children.title: Propagation-Cost Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Search regimes where stronger maintained consistency incurs disproportionate propagation cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Propagation-Cost Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case boundary for increasing maintained-consistency strength in finite CSPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Propagation strength alone gives no polynomial-time guarantee. For an extensional constraint \(c\), checking generalized-arc support by direct tuple scanning can require examining \(|T_c|\) tuples, and \(|T_c|\) may be exponential in \(|\operatorname{scope}(c)|\) under an implicit domain-based size measure. More generally, enforcing a stronger local consistency can require time or space exponential in its consistency width or constraint arity. Consequently, replacing a weaker closure by a dominating closure may reduce the search tree yet increase total time or memory; escalation is beneficial only when saved search exceeds its additional propagation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stronger propagation may shrink search but require exponential work in arity or consistency width, so filtering dominance does not imply time or memory improvement.
assumptions_latex: Constraint arity or consistency width is not fixed.
Constraints may be represented intensionally or by exponentially large tuple sets.
Propagation cost includes support testing and stored intermediate relations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stronger maintained consistency has no unconditional polynomial-time or total-runtime dominance over weaker propagation.

notation.meaning: Set of allowed tuples for extensional constraint c.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The qualitative tradeoff is credible, but the exponential-cost claims depend on the input representation, consistency notion, and meaning of consistency width. An authoritative source specifying those parameters is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Breadth-First Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Level-order complete traversal of a propagation-pruned finite CSP search tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a FIFO queue with the propagated root state at depth \(0\). Repeatedly remove the oldest state \(S\). If \(S\) is a solution, output it; if propagation proves \(S\) inconsistent, discard it. Otherwise choose a branching disjunction whose children exhaust the solutions represented by \(S\), propagate every child, and append each nonfailed child to the queue. Return failure when the queue becomes empty. For finite branching and a solution at finite depth, breadth-first search eventually reaches a shallowest solution; on a finite tree it terminates with failure exactly when no solution exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A FIFO frontier explores propagated states by nondecreasing depth, finds a shallowest solution, and is complete on finite-branching trees with finite-depth solutions.
assumptions_latex: Every node has finitely many children.
Branching is exhaustive and propagation is sound.
Each node is processed in finite time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The first returned solution has minimum search depth, and the traversal is complete for finite-depth solutions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The FIFO traversal, shallowest-depth result, and stated completeness conditions are mathematically standard and fit the algorithm container, but no inspectable source is provided.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Best-First Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single global priority frontier over propagated CP search states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain one global priority queue \(\mathrm{OPEN}\), initialized with the propagated root. Repeatedly remove a state \(S\) of minimum key \(k(S)\), using a fixed tie rule. Output \(S\) if it is a solution; discard it if failed; otherwise generate an exhaustive propagated partition of its descendants and insert every nonfailed child into \(\mathrm{OPEN}\). Return failure when \(\mathrm{OPEN}=\varnothing\). The traversal is complete provided every finite-depth solution node has only finitely many generated nodes selected before it; without this fairness condition, an infinite sequence of better-key nodes can starve a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single priority queue always expands the globally best keyed state; completeness additionally requires that no finite-depth solution can be starved indefinitely.
assumptions_latex: Branching is exhaustive, propagation is sound, and node processing terminates.
The priority and tie rules are deterministic.
Every solution node has finitely many predecessors under the induced expansion order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm finds a solution if one exists at finite depth and the expansion order is fair.

notation.meaning: Global frontier of generated, unexpanded states.
Priority key of state S, minimized by selection.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The global-priority algorithm is coherent, and it appropriately notes starvation, but the exact fairness condition and completeness formulation require an authoritative best-first-search source.

knowledge_statements.title: Interleaved Best-First Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fair alternation among multiple best-first frontiers or priority policies.
