knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The diagnostic measures incumbent improvement, candidate novelty, and repair success over a window, then classifies stagnation as low-novelty, repair-limited, or unclassified.
assumptions_latex: Each \(s_i\in\{0,1\}\) indicates whether iteration \(i\) produced a feasible repair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta\le\delta\) triggers a stagnation report classified using \(\nu\) and \(\rho\).

notation.meaning: Incumbent objective improvement over the window.
Number of distinct generated candidates per iteration.
Fraction of iterations producing feasible repairs.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: operational diagnostic built from common LNS run statistics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is plausible, but its novelty statistic, thresholds, and diagnostic labels are uncited. It also does not specify whether low novelty and repair limitation may be reported simultaneously or how overlapping labels are prioritized.

children.title: Destruction-Escalation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Covers conditions motivating broader destruction without entering excessive-relaxation regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Destruction-Escalation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive boundary for increasing destruction after persistent low-novelty stagnation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d_t\) be the destruction size at iteration \(t\), bounded by \(d_{\max}\), and let \(K\ge1\). An escalation boundary is crossed at \(t\) when the stagnation diagnostic reports \(\Delta_j\le\delta\) and \(\nu_j\le\nu_0\) for each of the last \(K\) diagnostic windows, while \(d_t<d_{\max}\). The prescribed update is \[d_{t+1}=\min\{d_{\max},\lceil\gamma d_t\rceil\},\qquad \gamma>1.\] If any boundary predicate fails, this rule leaves the destruction size unchanged: \(d_{t+1}=d_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Destruction is escalated when low-improvement, low-novelty stagnation persists for several windows and the current relaxation size remains below its cap.
assumptions_latex: \(1\le d_t\le d_{\max}\).
\(K\ge1\) and \(\gamma>1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{t+1}=\min\{d_{\max},\lceil\gamma d_t\rceil\}\) exactly when the escalation predicate holds.

notation.meaning: Required number of consecutive stagnant diagnostic windows.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit adaptive-control boundary for LNS destruction size

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits a destruction-escalation boundary, but the consecutive-window predicate and multiplicative update are policy-specific and have no supporting citation.

children.title: Over-Destruction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers neighborhoods that discard too much useful incumbent structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Over-Destruction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational regime combining weak incumbent retention with excessive repair cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an LNS instance have \(n\) variables, incumbent \(x\), destruction set \(D\), repair cost \(C(D,x)\), and budget \(B>0\). For thresholds \(r_0\in[0,1]\) and \(q_0\in[0,1]\), define the retained fraction \(r(D)=1-|D|/n\) and the budget-overrun probability \(q(D,x)=\Pr(C(D,x)>B)\). The run is in an over-destruction regime at \(x\) when every operator selected with positive probability satisfies \[r(D)\le r_0\quad\text{and}\quad q(D,x)\ge q_0.\] The regime therefore combines little fixed incumbent structure with predictably expensive repair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over-destruction occurs when supported operators preserve little of the incumbent and their repair subproblems exceed the allotted budget with high probability.
assumptions_latex: The model has finitely many variables.
Repair cost and budget use the same resource measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r(D)\le r_0\) and \(\Pr(C(D,x)>B)\ge q_0\) for every supported operator.

notation.meaning: Fraction of variables retained from the incumbent.
Resource cost of repairing destruction set D at x.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: operationalizes over-destruction through retention and repair cost

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the over-destruction leaf, but combining retained-variable fraction and budget-overrun probability is an uncited operational convention. The probability model for repair cost also requires authoritative specification.

children.title: Restart-Like Search Collapse
children.top_down_role: Covers LNS behavior that becomes indistinguishable from repeated near-global restarts.

knowledge_statements.title: Restart-Like Search Collapse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel-based boundary where LNS transitions become nearly incumbent-independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_d(x,\cdot)\) be the distribution of the next feasible candidate generated from incumbent \(x\) using destruction level \(d\), and let \(R_d\) be a reference distribution independent of \(x\). Restart-like collapse occurs at tolerance \(\eta\in[0,1]\) when \[\sup_{x\in F}\left\|P_d(x,\cdot)-R_d\right\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\eta.\] Consequently, for any two incumbents \(x,x'\in F\), \(\|P_d(x,\cdot)-P_d(x',\cdot)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le2\eta\). At \(\eta=0\), candidate generation is exactly incumbent-independent and is distributionally a restart.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search becomes restart-like when the next-candidate distribution is uniformly close to an incumbent-independent distribution; exact equality yields genuine distributional restarting.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is finite.
All transition distributions are defined on the same candidate space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{x\in F}\|P_d(x,\cdot)-R_d\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\eta\) characterizes restart-like collapse.

notation.meaning: Next-candidate transition distribution from incumbent x.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formal Markov-kernel criterion for restart-like behavior

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The total-variation formulation and its triangle-inequality consequence are coherent, and failure_boundary fits the container, but no source establishes this as an LNS restart-collapse criterion.

children.title: Repair-Guidance Loss
children.top_down_role: Covers erosion of incumbent-derived information that should focus the repair subproblem.

knowledge_statements.title: Repair-Guidance Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic formulation of lost dependence on preserved incumbent structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a random incumbent, let \(U=X_{-D}\) be the assignment preserved outside destruction set \(D\), and let \(Y\) be the repaired candidate, with failure represented by a distinguished outcome. Repair guidance is lost at tolerance \(\eta\ge0\) when the conditional mutual information satisfies \[I(U;Y\mid D)\le\eta.\] At the sharp boundary \(\eta=0\), \(U\) and \(Y\) are conditionally independent given \(D\); hence preserving incumbent variables conveys no distributional information about the repair output beyond knowing the selected destruction set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repair guidance is lost when preserved incumbent assignments carry negligible conditional information about the repaired candidate; zero information gives conditional independence.
assumptions_latex: \((X,D,Y)\) has a well-defined joint distribution.
Failure is included as an output value of \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(X_{-D};Y\mid D)\le\eta\), with conditional independence when \(\eta=0\).

notation.meaning: Incumbent assignment retained outside the destroyed variables.
Repair output, including a failure outcome.
Conditional mutual information measuring repair guidance.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: information-theoretic operationalization of incumbent guidance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-information implication is standard when the relevant random variables and mutual information are properly defined, but this LNS interpretation is uncited. Because the dimension of X_{-D} can depend on D, a common measurable state space or tagged representation should also be specified.

children.title: Destruction-Reduction Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Covers conditions motivating tighter neighborhoods after repair effectiveness collapses.

knowledge_statements.title: Destruction-Reduction Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive boundary for reducing destruction when repair reliability or cost is unacceptable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d_t\ge d_{\min}\) be the destruction size, and over the latest \(W\) repairs let \(\rho_t\) be the feasible-repair fraction and \(\bar C_t\) the mean repair cost. Given thresholds \(\rho_0\in[0,1]\), \(B>0\), and \(\beta\in(0,1)\), the destruction-reduction boundary is crossed when \[\rho_t<\rho_0\quad\text{or}\quad \bar C_t>B.\] If it is crossed and \(d_t>d_{\min}\), update \(d_{t+1}=\max\{d_{\min},\lfloor\beta d_t\rfloor\}\); otherwise set \(d_{t+1}=d_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Destruction is reduced when recent repairs are insufficiently reliable or too costly, subject to a minimum relaxation size.
assumptions_latex: \(W\ge1\) completed repair attempts are observed.
\(0<\beta<1\) and \(1\le d_{\min}\le d_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{t+1}=\max\{d_{\min},\lfloor\beta d_t\rfloor\}\) when the reduction predicate holds and \(d_t>d_{\min}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit adaptive-control boundary based on repair success and cost

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary condition matches the leaf, but the disjunctive trigger, thresholds, and multiplicative reduction rule are uncited policy choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Repair-Subproblem Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case NP-hardness inherited when an LNS operator may destroy every decision variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an explicitly encoded finite-domain constraint-optimization class whose threshold decision problem asks whether there is a feasible assignment \(z\) satisfying \(f(z)\le K\). For incumbent \(x\) and destruction set \(D\subseteq V\), define the corresponding repair decision problem by adding the restrictions \(z_{V\setminus D}=x_{V\setminus D}\). If the destruction family permits \(D=V\), these restrictions are vacuous, so the original threshold instance is identically an unrestricted repair instance. Consequently, if the original threshold problem is NP-hard, then the unrestricted LNS repair decision problem is NP-hard. In particular, it has no polynomial-time algorithm for all encoded instances unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the operator may destroy every variable, an unrestricted repair instance can be identical to the original threshold decision problem. Thus NP-hard model classes have NP-hard unrestricted repair, and no polynomial-time algorithm solves every encoded instance unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: The original, explicitly encoded threshold decision problem is NP-hard.
The destruction family contains \(D=V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unrestricted LNS repair decision problem is NP-hard and therefore has no polynomial-time algorithm for all instances unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

notation.meaning: Variables relaxed by the destruction operator.
Objective threshold in the decision problem.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: identity reduction obtained by destroying all variables

knowledge_statements.title: Disconnected Neighborhood Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reachability graph induced by supported destroy-and-repair transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the finite feasible set and let \(\mathcal D\) be the support of the destruction-operator portfolio. Define the directed neighborhood graph \(G_{\mathcal D}=(F,E)\) by \[(x,y)\in E\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists D\in\mathcal D\text{ such that }y\in N_D(x)\text{ and the repair rule can return }y\text{ with positive probability}.\] The LNS neighborhood graph is disconnected in the search-relevant directed sense when \(G_{\mathcal D}\) is not strongly connected. Equivalently, there exist \(u,v\in F\) such that no directed path leads from \(u\) to \(v\). From an initial incumbent \(x_0\), repeated supported transitions can generate only vertices reachable from \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The LNS neighborhood graph links incumbents to repairs obtainable with positive probability. Failure of strong connectivity means that at least one feasible state cannot be reached from another, and search from an initial incumbent remains within its reachable set.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is finite.
Operator and repair supports are fixed when defining the graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(G_{\mathcal D}\) is not strongly connected, then there exist \(u,v\in F\) such that \(v\) is not reachable from \(u\).

notation.meaning: Directed graph of supported LNS transitions.
Feasible neighborhood formed by destroying D at x.

source_refs.locator: 2.7 Primal Bounds: Greedy and Local Search p. 34

source_witnesses.locator: 2.7 Primal Bounds: Greedy and Local Search p. 34

knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Portfolio Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reachability bias caused by zero or unequal selection probabilities over destruction operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let destruction operators \(D_1,\ldots,D_m\) be selected with probabilities \(p_1,\ldots,p_m\), and let \(P_i(x,y)\) be the repair transition kernel for operator \(D_i\). The portfolio kernel is \[P(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_iP_i(x,y).\] Its transition graph contains exactly those arcs \((x,y)\) for which \(p_iP_i(x,y)>0\) for some \(i\). Hence assigning \(p_i=0\) removes every arc unique to \(D_i\); unequal positive probabilities also alter path probabilities and expected hitting times, even when the reachable vertex set is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A portfolio's selection probabilities determine its effective transition graph; zero weights remove unique moves, while unequal positive weights change path probabilities and expected hitting times.
assumptions_latex: Each \(P_i\) is a transition kernel on the same finite feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(x,y)>0\) if and only if \(p_iP_i(x,y)>0\) for at least one \(i\).

notation.meaning: Selection probability of destruction operator i.
Repair transition kernel induced by operator i.
Mixture transition kernel of the operator portfolio.

knowledge_statements.title: LNS Incompleteness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp reachability obstruction to eventual discovery of a global optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(F,E)\) be the directed graph of all positive-probability LNS transitions under a fixed operator portfolio and repair rule, and let \(R(x_0)\) be the vertices reachable from initial incumbent \(x_0\). If every global minimizer lies outside \(R(x_0)\), then for every iteration \(t\), \[\Pr\!\left(X_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\mid X_0=x_0\right)=0.\] Consequently, the probability of ever visiting a global minimizer is zero, and this LNS configuration is incomplete from \(x_0\). Conversely, graph reachability of an optimum is necessary but not sufficient for almost-sure discovery unless the scheduling and repair probabilities prevent starvation of its finite paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LNS is incomplete from an initial incumbent when no global optimum is reachable through its positive-probability transitions. Reachability is necessary but does not alone ensure almost-sure discovery.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is finite.
The operator portfolio and repair transition kernel are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\cap R(x_0)=\varnothing\) implies that the probability of ever visiting a global minimizer is zero.

children.title: Favorable Decomposition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers problem structures where partial relaxation isolates useful, manageable neighborhoods.

assumptions_latex: \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_m\) is a finite-domain constraint model with objective \(f\).
Each destruction operator frees a block \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and repair solves the induced subproblem exactly.
Cross-block constraints admit propagation or conditioning through a boundary of bounded size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The LNS repair effort is localized while improvements spanning individual blocks remain reachable.

notation.meaning: block of variables freed by destruction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient structural regime for decomposition-aligned finite-domain LNS.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the variables be partitioned into blocks \(X_1,\ldots,X_m\). A favorable decomposition regime holds when each neighborhood frees one or a few blocks \(B\), fixing all remaining variables; the resulting repair problem contains only the freed variables and a boundary interface of bounded size; and every improving solution \(y\) reachable from an incumbent \(x\) can be connected to \(x\) by finitely many such block repairs whose intermediate assignments are feasible and nonworsening. Under exact repair, each iteration then solves a localized subproblem, while the neighborhood family retains a path to every improvement admitted by the block decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LNS is decomposition-favorable when repairs remain localized by small interfaces and blockwise neighborhoods retain feasible, nonworsening paths to improvements.

children.title: Repair-Compatible Neighborhood Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers settings where released subproblems remain sufficiently informative and practically repairable.

assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a feasible incumbent of a finite-domain constraint optimization problem.
A neighborhood fixes variables outside a destroyed set \(B\) and repairs variables in \(B\).
The repair procedure is complete on the induced subproblem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every target improvement covered by the regime can be produced by at least one tractable repair neighborhood.
review_flags: A direct source defining repair-compatible LNS regimes is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition linking destruction choices to exact finite-domain repair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an incumbent \(x\in F\) and destroyed set \(B\), define the repair set by \(R_B(x)=\{y\in F:y_i=x_i\text{ for every }i\notin B\}\). A neighborhood family \(\mathcal B\) is repair-compatible on a target set \(T(x)\subseteq F\) when, for every \(y\in T(x)\), some \(B\in\mathcal B\) satisfies \(y\in R_B(x)\), and the induced constraint problem defining \(R_B(x)\) lies within the completeness and resource regime of the repair procedure. Thus every targeted improvement is both represented by a neighborhood and recoverable by its repair search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A neighborhood regime is repair-compatible when every targeted improvement lies in some induced repair set that the chosen repair method can solve completely.

knowledge_statements.title: Sound Branch Pruning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility- or incumbent-preserving pruning criterion for a constraint-search node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a constraint problem and let \(S(N)\) be the solutions of \(P\) consistent with the decisions at node \(N\). Relative to a search objective, let \(S_{\mathrm{rel}}(N)\subseteq S(N)\) denote the solutions that the search must preserve. A pruning certificate \(c_N\) is sound when its validity entails \(S_{\mathrm{rel}}(N)=\varnothing\). For feasibility search, \(S_{\mathrm{rel}}(N)=S(N)\). For minimization with incumbent value \(U\), if only improving solutions must be preserved, then \(S_{\mathrm{rel}}(N)=\{x\in S(N):f(x)<U\}\); consequently, a valid node lower bound \(L(N)\ge U\) soundly excludes the node from further improvement search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch pruning is sound when a valid certificate proves that the node contains no solution relevant to the search objective; this means no solution for feasibility search and no incumbent-improving solution for optimization search.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is the original constraint problem and \(N\) is a search node.
\(S(N)\) is the set of solutions of \(P\) consistent with the decisions at \(N\).
\(S_{\mathrm{rel}}(N)\) is the subset of node solutions that the current feasibility or optimization objective requires the search to preserve.
For minimization, \(U\) is the incumbent objective value and \(L(N)\) is a valid lower bound for every solution in \(S(N)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pruning \(N\) is sound whenever a valid certificate establishes \(S_{\mathrm{rel}}(N)=\varnothing\).

valid lower bound at node N

assumptions_latex: Every propagator is contracting and solution-preserving on the current domains.
Each branching disjunction covers every assignment remaining after propagation.
A branch is discarded only by a sound failure or optimization-bound certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The composed propagation-and-search procedure preserves every solution until it is returned or lies in an unexplored covering branch.
review_flags: A direct CP search metatheory source with the composition theorem is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compositional soundness for propagation followed by exhaustive branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a domain state and let propagation produce \(p(D)\subseteq D\) with \(\operatorname{Sol}(p(D))=\operatorname{Sol}(D)\). Suppose branching produces children \(D_1,\ldots,D_k\subseteq p(D)\) satisfying \(\operatorname{Sol}(p(D))=\bigcup_{j=1}^k\operatorname{Sol}(D_j)\). If every discarded child has a valid certificate that it contains no relevant solution, then propagation followed by recursive exploration of the remaining children is sound: no relevant solution represented by \(D\) is removed except by a valid certificate, and every returned assignment satisfies the original constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solution-preserving propagation composed with covering branches and certified pruning yields a sound constraint-search procedure.
knowledge_statements.title: Sound Propagation–Search Composition

assumptions_latex: The current node has decision stack \(d_1,\ldots,d_k\).
A detected failure has a valid explanation \(E\subseteq\{d_1,\ldots,d_k\}\).
The retained prefix omits at least one decision from \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Retracting beyond the deepest retained decision in the explanation cannot discard a solution consistent with the retained prefix.
review_flags: A direct source for explanation-based backtracking or backjumping is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness condition for explanation-directed backtracking or backjumping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d_1,\ldots,d_k\) be the current decisions and let \(E\subseteq\{d_1,\ldots,d_k\}\) be a valid failure explanation, meaning that the original constraints together with all decisions in \(E\) are inconsistent. Retraction to a prefix ending before the deepest decision of \(E\) is sound provided search subsequently explores every alternative not excluded by a valid learned consequence. Indeed, only the inconsistent conjunction \(\bigwedge_{d\in E}d\) may be excluded; assignments compatible with the retained prefix but violating some member of \(E\) remain eligible for exploration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure-directed retraction is sound when a valid explanation justifies the jump and alternatives not excluded by that explanation remain searchable.
knowledge_statements.title: Sound Failure-Directed Retraction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property appropriately conditions soundness on a valid failure explanation and continued exploration of alternatives, but no authoritative explanation-based backtracking source is supplied.

children.title: Sound Nogood Learning
children.top_down_role: Covers validity boundaries for learned nogoods used during search.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is the conjunction of the original constraints.
\(L=\ell_1\land\cdots\land\ell_k\) is a conjunction of decision or domain literals.
The solver establishes \(C\models\neg L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Adding the nogood \(\neg L\) preserves exactly the solution set of \(C\).
review_flags: A direct authoritative source on CP nogood learning is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical criterion for solution-preserving nogood acquisition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a solver derives \(C\models\neg(\ell_1\land\cdots\land\ell_k)\). It may soundly learn the nogood \(N=
eg\ell_1\lor\cdots\lor
eg\ell_k\). Since every model of \(C\) satisfies \(N\), the augmented problem has the same models: \(\operatorname{Mod}(C\land N)=\operatorname{Mod}(C)\). The learned nogood may therefore propagate literals, reject a node containing every \(\ell_i\), or justify retraction, but it may not exclude any solution of the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A learned nogood is sound precisely when it is entailed by the original constraints, so adding it preserves all original solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Sound Nogood Learning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The entailment criterion and model-preservation equation are mathematically coherent and fit sound nogood learning, but the record lacks the required authoritative CP nogood-learning source.

children.title: Sound Explanation Learning
children.top_down_role: Covers validity boundaries for learned explanatory objects.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is the original constraint conjunction and \(A\) is the active context.
A propagation or failure produces consequence \(q\).
The learned explanation uses only semantically defined literals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The explanation is sound when \(C\models A\rightarrow q\), equivalently \(C\land A\land\neg q\) is inconsistent.
review_flags: A direct authoritative source on explanation-based constraint propagation is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entailment criterion for learned propagation and failure explanations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An explanation \(A\rightarrow q\) learned from propagation is sound exactly when \(C\models A\rightarrow q\). For a failure, take \(q=\bot\), so soundness requires \(C\models
eg A\). Adding the explanatory implication then preserves the models of \(C\). Any subsequent propagation, conflict analysis, or backjump based on the explanation is sound only under contexts satisfying every antecedent literal in \(A\); weakening \(A\) is permitted only if the weakened implication is independently entailed by \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explanation is sound when the original constraints entail its consequence under every listed antecedent; failure explanations must entail contradiction.
knowledge_statements.title: Sound Explanation Learning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The entailment condition fits sound explanation learning and distinguishes propagation from failure explanations, but it has no direct authoritative source.

children.title: Learning–Pruning Soundness Interface
children.top_down_role: Covers the use of learned information as justification for later propagation, pruning, or retraction.

assumptions_latex: Every learned constraint \(L\) satisfies \(C\models L\).
The pruning engine removes a node only when its context contradicts \(C\land L_1\land\cdots\land L_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Learning followed by pruning preserves all models of the original constraints.
review_flags: A direct source for the learning-pruning composition result is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compositional soundness boundary between entailed learning and branch deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every learned constraint \(L_i\) satisfy \(C\models L_i\). Then \(\operatorname{Mod}(C\land L_1\land\cdots\land L_t)=\operatorname{Mod}(C)\). If a node with context \(A_N\) is pruned only after establishing \(C\land L_1\land\cdots\land L_t\land A_N\models\bot\), that node contains no model of \(C\). Hence the learning-pruning interface is sound. Conversely, using a learned constraint not entailed by \(C\), or applying an explanation outside its antecedent context, does not provide a sound pruning certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entailed learned constraints may safely drive pruning; non-entailed constraints or explanations used outside their context may delete valid solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Learning–Pruning Soundness Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem correctly links entailed learning with contradiction-based pruning and fits the interface container, but the composition result is uncited.

assumptions_latex: There are finitely many variables, each with a finite initial domain.
Propagation terminates at every node.
Every nonterminal branch strictly reduces the remaining assignment set, and no node is revisited indefinitely.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^n D_i\), where every \(D_i\) is finite. Associate each node \(N\) with a set \(R(N)\subseteq\Omega\) of remaining assignments. Suppose propagation terminates, every branch has finitely many children, child sets cover the parent set, and along every edge to a nonterminal child \(N'\) one has \(R(N')\subsetneq R(N)\). If the search policy does not regenerate nodes indefinitely, then every root-to-leaf path and the entire search tree are finite. Consequently exhaustive traversal terminates after returning solutions or proving failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite domains, terminating propagation, strictly reducing branches, and absence of indefinite revisitation guarantee termination of exhaustive constraint search.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Domain Search Termination

assumptions_latex: Branching disjunctions cover the assignments remaining at each node.
Propagation and pruning are sound.
Every generated, unpruned node is eventually expanded unless a solution is returned under the chosen search objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every solution is eventually reached, or every solution-relevant branch is finitely certified as exhausted.
review_flags: A direct source for fair branching and completeness in constraint search is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness under fair node selection, including potentially infinite search trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that for each expanded node \(N\), its children \(N_1,\ldots,N_k\) satisfy \(S(N)=\bigcup_{j=1}^k S(N_j)\), and that only nodes with \(S(N)=\varnothing\) are pruned. A node-selection policy is fair when every node that remains continuously on the frontier is selected after finitely many further selections. Under this fairness condition, every solution lying at finite depth is eventually reached. If all solution-relevant paths are finite, exhaustive fair search is complete: it returns a solution when one exists and, when the tree is finitely exhausted, correctly reports unsatisfiability otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Covering branches, sound pruning, and fair node selection ensure that every solution at finite depth is eventually reached.
knowledge_statements.title: Fair-Branching Completeness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem carefully limits eventual reachability to finite-depth solutions and unsatisfiability reporting to finite exhaustion, but no direct constraint-search completeness source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Enumeration Completeness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duplicate-free enumeration in a finite, exhaustive constraint search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) be the complete assignment vector and let \(S\) be the finite solution set of the original constraint problem. Suppose search is sound, complete, and finitely terminating. After returning \(x\in S\), suppose the enumeration procedure either continues only through unexplored regions disjoint from \(x\) or adds the enumeration exclusion \(X\ne x\), which removes exactly \(x\) and no member of \(S\setminus\{x\}\). If no other solution is excluded, then after each output step the output set \(O_t\subseteq S\) has no duplicates and every member of \(S\setminus O_t\) remains represented by the search frontier. When the frontier is finitely exhausted, \(O_t=S\), so every solution has been returned exactly once.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sound, complete, finitely terminating search enumerates every solution exactly once when each returned complete assignment alone is excluded and every other solution remains represented by the frontier.
assumptions_latex: \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) is the complete assignment vector and \(S\) is the finite solution set.
The search is sound, complete, exhaustive, and finitely terminating.
After returning \(x\in S\), the procedure excludes exactly \(x\), either structurally through disjoint unexplored branches or by adding \(X\ne x\).
No solution in \(S\setminus\{x\}\) is removed by the exclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output sequence is duplicate-free and its final output set equals \(S\).

notation.meaning: solution set of the original problem
set of solutions output through step t

review_flags: The cited partial-enumeration section should be checked for explicit all-solutions coverage.

assumptions_latex: Each search episode uses sound propagation and pruning.
Restart limits are unbounded along a subsequence, or retained state guarantees equivalent cumulative exploration.
Every finite solution-reaching search prefix is eventually permitted and selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Restarts do not destroy completeness: every solution with a finite witness path is eventually reached.

notation.meaning: resource limit of restart episode k
finite search prefix leading to a solution

review_flags: A direct authoritative source on completeness under restart schedules is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness criterion for restarted finite-domain search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider restart episodes with resource limits \(b_1,b_2,\ldots\). Suppose every solution \(x\) has a finite sound search prefix \(\pi_x\) of cost \(c(\pi_x)\), and the restart policy is fair in the sense that some episode permits at least \(c(\pi_x)\) work and makes every decision sequence of that finite prefix eligible for selection. Then \(x\) is eventually reached. In particular, completeness follows when \(\sup_k b_k=\infty\) and branching choices are fairly diversified. A permanently bounded schedule without cumulative coverage need not be complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restarted search remains complete when budgets and branching are fair enough to realize every finite solution-reaching search prefix.
knowledge_statements.title: Restart Completeness

children.title: Incumbent Quality Progression
children.top_down_role: Covers the role of progressively improved feasible incumbents in optimization search.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(F\) is finite, and the problem is \(\min\{f(x):x\in F\}\).
Each incumbent \(x_k\) is feasible, and it is replaced only by a feasible point having strictly smaller objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_{k+1}\le U_k\) for every incumbent update, and every strict replacement satisfies \(U_{k+1}<U_k\).

notation.meaning: incumbent after the kth accepted update

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization convention with strict-improvement incumbent replacement.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem \(\min\{f(x):x\in F\}\), let \(x_k\in F\) be the incumbent after the \(k\)-th accepted update and set \(U_k=f(x_k)\). If an update accepts \(y\in F\) only when \(f(y)<U_k\), then \(x_{k+1}=y\) and \(U_{k+1}<U_k\); if no replacement occurs, the incumbent value remains \(U_k\). Consequently, the incumbent-value sequence is nonincreasing and every recorded replacement is a strict improvement. Because \(F\) is finite, only finitely many strict incumbent improvements can occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite minimization search, accepting only strictly better feasible solutions makes incumbent values decrease monotonically and permits only finitely many strict improvements.
knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent Quality Progression

children.title: Objective-Bound Validity
children.top_down_role: Covers validity requirements for bounds used to exclude improving solutions.

assumptions_latex: For every live search node \(v\), its completion set is \(F_v\subseteq F\).
The computed value \(L(v)\) satisfies \(L(v)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in F_v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(L(v)\ge U\), then \(F_v\) contains no point with objective value strictly below \(U\).

notation.meaning: feasible completions represented by node v
objective value of a feasible incumbent

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and pruning condition for minimization lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a search node \(v\), a scalar \(L(v)\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}\) is a valid minimization bound precisely when \(L(v)\le f(x)\) for every feasible completion \(x\in F_v\). Given a feasible incumbent of value \(U\), the node may be discarded by objective bounding whenever \(L(v)\ge U\), since then every \(x\in F_v\) satisfies \(f(x)\ge U\). Bound validity is independent of how \(L(v)\) is computed; relaxation, propagation, or dual reasoning is admissible only if the displayed inequality is preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node lower bound is valid when it does not exceed any completion value; a node bounded at or above the incumbent cannot improve it.

children.title: Search-Space Exhaustion
children.top_down_role: Covers structural coverage of all regions capable of containing a better solution.

assumptions_latex: The problem is \(\min\{f(x):x\in F\}\), and the generated rooted search tree is finite.
The root \(r\) satisfies \(F_r=F\), and replacing a node \(v\) by children \(C(v)\) preserves coverage: \(F_v=\bigcup_{w\in C(v)}F_w\).
Every leaf represents either no feasible completion or one fully assigned candidate whose feasibility and objective value are examined.

A nonleaf node is discarded without branching only after proving \(F_v=\varnothing\) or establishing a valid lower bound \(L(v)\) with \(L(v)\ge U_t\), where \(U_t\) is the value of a feasible incumbent at that time.
The search terminates with no live nodes and with a final feasible incumbent \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x)=\min_{x\in F}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: feasible set of the minimization problem
feasible completions represented by search node v
incumbent objective value when a node is discarded

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{f(x):x\in F\}\). Let a finite rooted search tree represent \(F\), with root \(r\) satisfying \(F_r=F\). Suppose every branching step replaces a node \(v\) by children \(C(v)\) satisfying \(F_v=\bigcup_{w\in C(v)}F_w\); every leaf is infeasible or is a fully assigned candidate whose feasibility and objective value are examined; and every nonleaf node discarded without branching is proved infeasible or has a valid lower bound at least the value of the incumbent then available. If the search terminates with no live nodes and final feasible incumbent \(\bar x\), then \(f(\bar x)=\min_{x\in F}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exhausting a finite, coverage-preserving search tree certifies that the final feasible incumbent is globally optimal when every unbranched removal is justified by infeasibility or a valid incumbent-excluding bound.

children.title: Optimality Certification Boundary
children.top_down_role: Covers when completed constraint-optimization search supports an optimality status.

assumptions_latex: A minimization search returns a feasible incumbent \(\bar x\) of value \(U\).
At termination an unexplored node \(v\) may still contain feasible completions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without proving \(F_v=\varnothing\) or \(L(v)\ge U\) for every residual node, feasibility of \(\bar x\) does not certify global optimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between a feasible incumbent and a global-optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Feasibility and incumbent stabilization alone do not certify optimality. Specifically, suppose a minimization search returns \(\bar x\in F\) with \(U=f(\bar x)\) while leaving a node \(v\) unresolved. If neither \(F_v=\varnothing\) nor a valid inequality \(L(v)\ge U\) has been established, then the maintained information is compatible with the existence of \(y\in F_v\) satisfying \(f(y)<U\). Thus certification is valid only after every residual region is exhausted, proved infeasible, or excluded by a valid objective bound; stopping earlier crosses the certification boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable feasible incumbent is not an optimality certificate while any unexplored region lacks either an infeasibility proof or a valid excluding bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimality Certification Boundary

assumptions_latex: Each internal node has at most \(b\ge 1\) children.
Every root-to-leaf path contains at most \(d\ge 0\) branching edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N\le\sum_{i=0}^{d}b^i\), which equals \(d+1\) for \(b=1\) and \((b^{d+1}-1)/(b-1)\) for \(b>1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case node count for a finite bounded-depth search tree.

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rooted search tree with maximum branching factor \(b\) and maximum depth \(d\), the number \(N_i\) of nodes at depth \(i\) satisfies \(N_i\le b^i\). Therefore the total generated-node count obeys \(N\le\sum_{i=0}^{d}b^i\). For \(b=1\), this gives \(N\le d+1\); for \(b>1\), it gives \(N\le(b^{d+1}-1)/(b-1)\). The bound is attained by the complete \(b\)-ary tree of depth \(d\), so no smaller worst-case bound follows from branching factor and depth alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A depth-d tree with branching factor at most b has at most the corresponding geometric-series number of nodes, and a complete tree attains it.
knowledge_statements.title: Search-Tree Size

source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

A search-tree-specific section, theorem, or page is required.

assumptions_latex: At node \(v\), propagation performs \(r_v\) propagator executions before reaching a fixpoint or failure.
The \(j\)-th execution costs \(c_{v,j}\) elementary operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{prop}}(v)=\sum_{j=1}^{r_v}c_{v,j}\le r_v c_{\max}(v)\).

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a search node \(v\), count propagation work as the sum of all propagator-execution costs incurred until a fixpoint or failure is detected. If \(r_v\) executions occur and execution \(j\) costs \(c_{v,j}\), then \(C_{\mathrm{prop}}(v)=\sum_{j=1}^{r_v}c_{v,j}\). Writing \(c_{\max}(v)=\max_{1\le j\le r_v}c_{v,j}\) gives \(C_{\mathrm{prop}}(v)\le r_v c_{\max}(v)\). Across generated nodes \(V\), total propagation work is \(\sum_{v\in V}C_{\mathrm{prop}}(v)\), separating per-node propagation cost from tree size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Per-node propagation cost is the sum of propagator execution costs through fixpoint or failure; total propagation work sums this quantity over generated nodes.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation-per-Node Cost

source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed sums are coherent as an accounting model, but the citation is only a generic algorithms-and-running-time section and does not support CP fixpoint propagation, propagator executions, or the separation of per-node propagation work from tree size. A CP-specific source is required.

assumptions_latex: A stored search node requires at most \(s\) memory units, excluding shared immutable model data.
The search depth is at most \(d\), and the maximum frontier size is \(w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Depth-first traversal uses \(O(ds)\) search-state memory, while explicit best-first frontier storage uses \(O(ws)\).

notation.meaning: maximum memory per stored search node
maximum number of simultaneously stored frontier nodes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary search-state memory, excluding shared model and learned constraints.

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each explicitly stored node state occupies at most \(s\) memory units. A depth-first traversal of depth at most \(d\) need retain one active root-to-current path together with bounded sibling bookkeeping, giving \(O(ds)\) search-state memory under reversible or copied states. A best-first traversal retaining a frontier of maximum cardinality \(w\) uses \(O(ws)\) memory for that frontier. These bounds exclude shared immutable model storage and learned constraints. If every stored state has size at least a positive constant multiple of \(s\), the corresponding bounds are \(\Theta(ds)\) and \(\Theta(ws)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Depth-first search stores a path-sized collection of states, whereas best-first search stores a frontier-sized collection; learned data and the shared model are separate.
knowledge_statements.title: Search Memory Cost

source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited section does not support the traversal-specific memory bounds. Moreover, the depth-first claim requires an explicit representation assumption ensuring only a constant amount of sibling or iterator state per level, and the stated Theta refinement requires attainment and simultaneous retention conditions not currently supplied. A suitable source is needed before fixing the exact formulation.

assumptions_latex: Learned object \(i\) has representation size \(\ell_i\) and remains active during node set \(A_i\).
Processing learned object \(i\) at node \(v\in A_i\) costs \(c_{i,v}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Peak learning space is at most \(\max_v\sum_{i:v\in A_i}\ell_i\), and cumulative learning time is \(\sum_i\sum_{v\in A_i}c_{i,v}\).

notation.meaning: nodes at which learned object i is retained
processing cost for learned object i at node v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive accounting model for retained learned constraints or nogoods.

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let learned object \(i\) occupy \(\ell_i\) memory units and be active at the nodes in \(A_i\). Under additive storage, learning space at node \(v\) is \(S_L(v)=\sum_{i:v\in A_i}\ell_i\), so peak learning space is \(S_L^{\max}=\max_v S_L(v)\). If examining, propagating, or maintaining object \(i\) at node \(v\in A_i\) costs \(c_{i,v}\), cumulative learning time is \(T_L=\sum_i\sum_{v\in A_i}c_{i,v}\). Retention or deletion policies change the sets \(A_i\), thereby coupling learning space and time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Learning space sums sizes of currently retained learned objects, while learning time sums their processing costs over all nodes where they remain active.
knowledge_statements.title: Learning Space–Time Cost

source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement defines peak additive learning space by equality, whereas the conclusion calls the same expression only an upper bound. More importantly, the generic complexity citation does not support learned-object retention, deletion, or processing costs in CP search. A CP learning or nogood-management source is required to determine the intended model.

children.title: Bound Computation Cost
children.top_down_role: Covers resource costs attributable to producing or strengthening search bounds.

assumptions_latex: A bound is computed at each node in a set \(B\).
Computing the bound at node \(v\in B\) costs \(c_B(v)\) elementary operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Total bound-computation work is \(T_B=\sum_{v\in B}c_B(v)\le |B|c_B^{\max}\).

notation.meaning: nodes where a bound is computed

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive running-time model for node-bound computations.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.3 Continuous bound versus Lagrangian bound p. 26

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be the set of generated nodes at which an objective bound is computed, and let \(c_B(v)\) be the elementary-operation cost of the chosen bounding procedure at node \(v\). The total bound-computation work is \(T_B=\sum_{v\in B}c_B(v)\). If \(c_B(v)\le c_B^{\max}\) for every \(v\in B\), then \(T_B\le |B|c_B^{\max}\). This accounting includes repeated solves or bound updates as separate costs and excludes propagation, branching, and repair unless those operations are internal to the declared bounding procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total bounding work is the sum of node-level bound costs and is at most the number of bounded nodes times the largest such cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Bound Computation Cost

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.3 Continuous bound versus Lagrangian bound p. 26

children.title: Repair-Subproblem Cost
children.top_down_role: Covers resource costs attributable to solving LNS repair subproblems.

assumptions_latex: Repair is invoked on a set \(R\) of search events or nodes.
Invocation \(r\in R\) costs \(c_R(r)\) elementary operations, including its internal subsearch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Total repair work is \(T_R=\sum_{r\in R}c_R(r)\le |R|c_R^{\max}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive cost model for heuristic or exact repair subproblems.

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) index all invocations of a repair subproblem during search, and let \(c_R(r)\) count the elementary operations used by invocation \(r\), including any internal propagation or subsearch assigned to repair. Then total repair work is \(T_R=\sum_{r\in R}c_R(r)\). If \(c_R(r)\le c_R^{\max}\) for all \(r\in R\), then \(T_R\le |R|c_R^{\max}\). When a repair invocation itself explores a tree with \(N_r\) nodes and per-node cost at most \(p_r\), one may use \(c_R(r)\le N_rp_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repair cost sums the work of all repair invocations; each invocation may itself be bounded by its subsearch size times its per-node cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Repair-Subproblem Cost

source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive formulas are plausible once repair invocations and their charged operations are fixed, but the cited generic running-time section does not support repair subproblems or the nested subsearch bound. A repair-, large-neighborhood-search-, or CP-search-specific source is required.

children.title: Cost-Balancing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers allocation tradeoffs between stronger bounding effort and deeper repair effort.

assumptions_latex: A policy parameter \(q\) controls the effort spent on bounding or repair.
The expected generated-node count is \(N(q)\), and expected extra work per generated node is \(c(q)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Total expected work is modeled by \(T(q)=N(q)c(q)\); an interior differentiable optimum satisfies \(N'(q)c(q)+N(q)c'(q)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable expected-cost model for tuning bounding or repair effort.

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\) parameterize effort devoted to bounding or repair, let \(N(q)\) be the expected number of generated nodes, and let \(c(q)>0\) be expected total per-node work including that effort. Under the multiplicative model \(T(q)=N(q)c(q)\), increasing effort is beneficial between \(q_1<q_2\) exactly when \(N(q_2)c(q_2)<N(q_1)c(q_1)\). If \(N\) and \(c\) are differentiable and an optimum \(q^*\) is interior, then \(N'(q^*)c(q^*)+N(q^*)c'(q^*)=0\), equivalently \(-N'(q^*)/N(q^*)=c'(q^*)/c(q^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extra bounding or repair effort is worthwhile only when its relative reduction in expected tree size offsets its relative increase in per-node work.
knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Balancing Regimes

source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The citation does not support this expected-cost tradeoff model. In addition, multiplying an expected node count by an expected per-node cost requires a declared modeling definition or probabilistic assumptions, and the logarithmic-derivative equivalence requires \(N(q^*)>0\), which is not stated. A supporting source is needed to determine the valid regime and hypotheses.

assumptions_latex: Algorithms \(A\) and \(B\) are evaluated on the same instance class \(\mathcal I\), machine model, stopping rule, and resource measure \(C\).
Both algorithms return answers satisfying the same correctness specification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) dominates \(B\) on \(\mathcal I\) when \(C_A(I)\le C_B(I)\) for every \(I\in\mathcal I\), with strict inequality for at least one instance.

notation.meaning: resource used by algorithm A on instance I
resource used by algorithm B on instance I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise dominance under a fixed correctness specification and cost model.

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an instance class \(\mathcal I\), a correctness specification, a common stopping rule, and a nonnegative resource measure \(C\), such as generated nodes, propagation executions, or elementary running time. A backtracking algorithm \(A\) weakly dominates \(B\) on \(\mathcal I\) when \(C_A(I)\le C_B(I)\) for every \(I\in\mathcal I\). It strictly dominates \(B\) when weak dominance holds and \(C_A(I)<C_B(I)\) for at least one \(I\in\mathcal I\). Comparisons using different correctness guarantees, stopping rules, or resource measures do not establish this dominance relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One backtracking algorithm dominates another only when it uses no more of a fixed resource on every comparable instance and less on at least one.
knowledge_statements.title: Backtracking-Algorithm Dominance

source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise comparison is internally coherent and definition is the appropriate content kind, but the generic algorithms-and-running-time locator does not establish this particular weak/strict dominance convention for backtracking algorithms. A comparative-search or algorithm-dominance source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Propagation-Strength Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers relative levels of inference achieved before or during branching.

knowledge_statements.title: Propagation-Strength Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise comparison of sound domain-reduction operators at a search node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\) be the set of domain states ordered by componentwise inclusion, and let \(P,Q:\mathcal D\to\mathcal D\) be sound, contracting, monotone, idempotent propagation operators. Define \(P\succeq Q\) when \(P(D)\subseteq Q(D)\) for every \(D\in\mathcal D\). The strict-strength regime is \(P\succ Q\) when \(P\succeq Q\) and strict inclusion holds for some state. The equivalence regime is \(P\equiv Q\) when \(P(D)=Q(D)\) for every state. Operators incomparable under \(\succeq\) form an incomparable-strength regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagation is stronger when it removes at least every value removed by another sound propagator on every domain state; equality and incomparability define the other regimes.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) are sound for the same constraint set.
Domain states are ordered by componentwise set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\succeq Q\iff (\forall D\in\mathcal D)\;P(D)\subseteq Q(D)\).

notation.meaning: P is at least as strong as Q

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the terminal container, and the notation is coherent, but no cited source supports this exact pointwise ordering of propagation operators or its regime terminology.

children.title: Search-Size Effects
children.top_down_role: Covers changes in explored nodes, failures, depth, or equivalent search-volume measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Size Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subtree comparison under fixed branching and node ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two depth-first searches using the same deterministic variable-value branching rule and the same child order. At every generated node with incoming domain state \(D\), suppose propagation satisfies \(P(D)\subseteq Q(D)\), and failure is detected whenever a domain becomes empty. Then every branch surviving under \(P\) also survives under \(Q\); hence the explored tree for \(P\) is a rooted subtree of that for \(Q\). Consequently its numbers of expanded nodes and leaves satisfy \(N_P\leq N_Q\). This comparison need not hold when propagation changes the branching choices or node order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With identical branching decisions, uniformly stronger propagation can only delete branches, so it cannot enlarge the explored search tree.
assumptions_latex: Both searches use identical deterministic branching and child ordering.
\(P(D)\subseteq Q(D)\) at every corresponding state.
Failure is recognized from an empty domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_P\subseteq T_Q\) and therefore \(N_P\leq N_Q\).

notation.meaning: Search tree generated with propagation P
Number of nodes expanded in that tree

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits Search-Size Effects, but the subtree claim needs a cited theorem with precise node correspondence and propagation assumptions. Using the same state-dependent deterministic rule does not by itself guarantee identical branching decisions after different propagation.

children.title: Strength–Size Tradeoff Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Covers comparative regimes where increased propagation effort changes search volume.

knowledge_statements.title: Strength–Size Tradeoff Frontiers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto frontier for propagation cost and resulting search size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a constraint instance, branching policy, node order, and stopping criterion. For each propagation regime \(P\) in a family \(\mathcal P\), let \(C(P)\) be its total propagation work and \(N(P)\) its number of expanded search nodes. A regime \(P\) is dominated by \(Q\) when \(C(Q)\leq C(P)\) and \(N(Q)\leq N(P)\), with at least one strict inequality. The strength–size tradeoff frontier is the set of nondominated points \(\{(C(P),N(P)):P\in\mathcal P\}\). Restricting \(C(P)\) to per-node work instead yields an explicitly different frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tradeoff frontier contains exactly those propagation regimes for which neither propagation work nor search size can improve without worsening the other.
assumptions_latex: The instance, branching policy, node order, and stopping criterion are fixed.
Propagation work is measured consistently across \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{(C(P),N(P)):P\in\mathcal P\text{ is nondominated}\}\).

notation.meaning: Total propagation work under regime P

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto-frontier definition and content kind fit the leaf, but the propagation-work metric and its interpretation as a strength–size frontier lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Cost-Reversal Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Covers settings where search reduction fails to offset the extra cost of stronger propagation.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Reversal Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Break-even condition between propagation regimes under an additive runtime model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For propagation regimes \(P\) and \(Q\), let \(c_P,c_Q>0\) be their mean propagation costs per expanded node, let \(N_P,N_Q\) be their expanded-node counts, and let \(h\geq0\) be equal nonpropagation overhead per node. Under the additive model \(T_R=(c_R+h)N_R\), the cost-reversal boundary is \((c_P+h)N_P=(c_Q+h)N_Q\). Regime \(P\) is faster precisely on the side satisfying \((c_P+h)N_P<(c_Q+h)N_Q\), even when \(c_P>c_Q\), provided its search-size reduction is sufficiently large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stronger but costlier propagator becomes preferable exactly when its reduction in expanded nodes offsets its greater per-node cost.
assumptions_latex: Runtime is modeled additively by propagation and common per-node overhead.
All costs and node counts are measured on the same instance and search policy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_P<T_Q\iff N_P/N_Q<(c_Q+h)/(c_P+h)\).

notation.meaning: Mean propagation cost per expanded node for regime R
Modeled total runtime for regime R

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits Cost-Reversal Boundaries and the algebra is correct when node counts are positive, but the additive runtime model and break-even interpretation require a specific source; the ratio conclusion also leaves the positivity of N_Q implicit.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering-Sensitive Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of propagation-dominance comparisons when branching order is adaptive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\succeq Q\) be propagation regimes, and let branching select the next variable from the propagated state. Pointwise strength alone does not imply \(N_P\leq N_Q\): stronger pruning may change selected variables, values, and subtree order, so the two searches need not have corresponding nodes. The subtree inclusion conclusion is guaranteed only when the branching decision and child order agree at every corresponding surviving state, or when a separate simulation establishes such correspondence. Thus adaptive ordering is a failure boundary for search-size dominance inferred solely from propagation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stronger propagation need not yield a smaller search when adaptive heuristics react to pruning and choose a different branching order.
assumptions_latex: \(P\succeq Q\) is interpreted pointwise on common domain states.
Branching may depend on the propagated domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\succeq Q\not\Rightarrow N_P\leq N_Q\) without an ordering-preservation or simulation condition.

notation.meaning: P is pointwise at least as strong as Q

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure-boundary is an appropriate kind for this container, but the nonimplication and the claimed sufficient correspondence condition require a cited comparison theorem or explicit published counterexample.

knowledge_statements.title: Learning–Restart Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic invariance and completeness conditions for learning with restarts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a finite-domain constraint instance. After each conflict, add a learned constraint \(L\) satisfying \(F\models L\), retain every learned constraint across restarts, and restart by discarding only the current partial assignment. Then learning and restarting preserve the solution set because \(\operatorname{Sol}(F)=\operatorname{Sol}(F\land L)\). If the branching and restart policy is fair—every unresolved finite branch is eventually explored or permanently excluded by an entailed learned constraint—the procedure is complete. Without retained learning or fairness, repeated restarts may revisit the same prefixes indefinitely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entailed learned constraints survive restarts without removing solutions; completeness additionally requires a fair policy that eventually explores or excludes every unresolved branch.
assumptions_latex: All variable domains are finite.
Every learned constraint is entailed by the original instance and retained.
The branching and restart schedule is fair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}(F)=\operatorname{Sol}(F\land\bigwedge_i L_i)\), and fair restarted search is complete.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits Learning–Restart Interactions. Solution-set preservation is standard, but the fairness condition is informal and the completeness conclusion needs a precise restart-search model and authoritative locator.

children.title: Search-Level Certificates
children.top_down_role: Navigation endpoints for certificates produced by search; proof-format design and checker construction are external.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directly checkable witness of finite-domain constraint satisfaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-domain constraint satisfaction problem with variables \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\), domains \(D_i\), and constraints \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\), a solution certificate is a total assignment \(a:X\to\bigcup_iD_i\). A verifier accepts exactly when \(a(x_i)\in D_i\) for every \(i\) and each constraint predicate satisfies \(C_j(a|_{\operatorname{scope}(C_j)})=\mathrm{true}\). Acceptance certifies that \(a\) is feasible. When each predicate is polynomial-time evaluable and assignments have polynomial encoding length, certificate verification is polynomial in the encoded instance and certificate sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution certificate is a complete assignment whose domain membership and every constraint can be checked directly.
assumptions_latex: The assignment gives one encoded value for every variable.
Each constraint predicate can be evaluated on its scope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\text{ is accepted}\iff (\forall i)\,a(x_i)\in D_i\land(\forall j)\,C_j(a)=\mathrm{true}\).

notation.meaning: Total assignment serving as the certificate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is the correct content kind and the feasibility witness is well specified, but no source supports the verification formulation or its polynomial-time qualification.

knowledge_statements.title: Unsatisfiability Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable exhaustive search tree whose leaves are locally refuted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An unsatisfiability certificate for a finite-domain constraint instance \(F\) is a finite rooted tree. Its root represents the initial domains; every internal node applies an exhaustive split whose child cases cover its parent case; and every leaf contains a checkable derivation of contradiction from \(F\) and the branch decisions on its path. A verifier checks each split-cover relation and every leaf derivation using sound inference rules. If all checks succeed, every total assignment belongs to a refuted leaf case, so \(F\) has no solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exhaustive tree of sound case splits, with a verifiable contradiction at every leaf, certifies that no solution exists.
assumptions_latex: Every internal split exhaustively covers its parent case.
Every leaf contradiction is derived by verifier-recognized sound rules.
The certificate tree is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Verify}(F,T)=\mathrm{accept}\Rightarrow\operatorname{Sol}(F)=\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and exhaustive-tree formulation fit the leaf, but certificate validity depends on a specified proof language, split encoding, and verifier-recognized inference system, none of which is sourced.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal witness paired with a certified global objective bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the minimization problem \(z^*=\min\{f(x):x\in S\}\), an optimality certificate consists of a feasible assignment \(\hat x\in S\) and a verifiable lower-bound certificate establishing \(f(x)\geq L\) for every \(x\in S\). If the verifier confirms feasibility, validates the global bound, and finds \(f(\hat x)=L\), then \(\hat x\) is globally optimal and \(z^*=L\). Equivalently, the bound component may certify unsatisfiability of \(S\cap\{x:f(x)<f(\hat x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible solution is certified optimal by a verified global lower bound equal to its objective value, or by excluding every strictly better solution.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem with feasible set \(S\).
Feasibility, objective evaluation, and the lower-bound derivation are checkable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\hat x\in S\land(\forall x\in S)\,f(x)\geq L\land f(\hat x)=L\Rightarrow z^*=f(\hat x)=L\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is the correct role, and the primal-witness plus matching global-bound condition is mathematically sound. An inspectable source for this certificate formulation and its unsatisfiability equivalent is absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Explanation-to-Proof Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of propagation explanations into independently checkable proof steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a propagation event derive literal \(\ell\) under antecedent literals \(A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}\). An explanation-to-proof interface emits a proof object encoding the implication \((a_1\land\cdots\land a_k)\Rightarrow\ell\), or equivalently the clause \(\neg a_1\lor\cdots\lor\neg a_k\lor\ell\). The interface is sound when every emitted implication is entailed by the modeled constraints and every explanation-combination operation corresponds to a verifier-approved inference rule. A conflict explanation derives the empty clause; a verifier checking the emitted steps thereby obtains an unsatisfiability certificate for the explored case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface converts each propagation explanation into an entailed clause and combines such clauses through verifier-approved rules, ending in contradiction for a refuted case.
assumptions_latex: Literals have a fixed semantics over the constraint model.
Each emitted explanation is entailed by the responsible constraint.
The checker recognizes every composition rule used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\models((\bigwedge_{a\in A}a)\Rightarrow\ell)\iff F\models(\bigvee_{a\in A}\neg a\lor\ell)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation fits the interface container, and the implication-to-clause equivalence is correct. The claims about explanation composition and obtaining an unsatisfiability certificate depend on a concrete proof format and checker that are not cited.

children.title: Search Complexity Regime Boundary
children.top_down_role: Only consequences for search organization are retained; structural and language-based CSP tractability classifications belong to the complexity chapter.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Width Search Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain CSP complexity parameterized by primal-graph treewidth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite-domain CSP have \(n\) variables, maximum domain size \(d\), and primal graph of treewidth at most \(w\). Given a width-\(w\) tree decomposition, dynamic programming over its bags decides satisfiability and recovers a solution, when one exists, using \(O(n d^{w+1})\) table entries and polynomial work per entry for explicitly represented constraints. Equivalently, search following a compatible elimination order and memoizing each separator state explores at most \(O(n d^{w+1})\) distinct bag assignments. Thus fixed \(w\) and bounded \(d\) define a polynomial-time search regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A CSP of bounded primal treewidth and bounded domain size is solvable in polynomial time by bag-based dynamic programming or equivalent memoized search.
assumptions_latex: The primal graph has a supplied tree decomposition of width at most \(w\).
Every variable domain has size at most \(d\).
Constraint checks on bag assignments take polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{distinct table states}=O(n d^{w+1})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Complexity-bound is appropriate, and the bounded-treewidth conclusion is standard, but the exact O(n d^{w+1}) state bound and equivalence with memoized search need an authoritative theorem locator and a precise constraint-representation model.

knowledge_statements.title: Backtrack-Free Consistency Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional consistency guarantee relative to a bounded-width variable ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite-domain CSP have an ordered primal graph whose induced width is \(w\). Suppose the CSP is strongly directionally \((w+1)\)-consistent along that ordering: whenever values assigned consistently to at most \(w\) earlier neighbors of the next variable satisfy all applicable constraints, the assignment extends to some value of that variable. Then chronological search instantiating variables in the ordering never encounters a dead end after making a locally consistent choice. Hence any consistent prefix extends successively to a complete solution, and no backtracking is required; if preprocessing detects inconsistency, the instance is unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along an ordering of induced width w, strong directional (w+1)-consistency makes every consistent prefix extendible, so chronological search needs no backtracking.
assumptions_latex: All domains are finite.
The chosen variable ordering has induced width \(w\).
The instance is strongly directionally \((w+1)\)-consistent along that ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{every consistent search prefix extends to a solution}\), so \(\text{backtracks}=0\).

notation.meaning: Induced width of the chosen ordering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits Backtrack-Free Consistency Regimes, but the exact ordering direction, definition of strong directional consistency, and claim that every consistent prefix extends must be checked against a specifically located theorem.

assumptions_latex: There are \(n\) binary decision variables and search branches on one previously unfixed variable at each internal node.
Propagation neither detects failure nor fixes an unbranched variable before every variable is assigned.
Every complete assignment must be examined before infeasibility is certified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The search examines \(2^n\) leaves and \(2^{n+1}-1\) total nodes; hence its worst-case running time is \(\Omega(2^n)\) when node processing costs at least a positive constant.

notation.meaning: Rooted search tree generated by propagation-guided branching.
Number of nodes in the search tree.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional boundary for binary depth-first CP search when propagation provides no pruning before complete assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a complete propagation-guided search on \(n\) binary variables. Suppose that every internal node branches into the two values of one unfixed variable, and that propagation neither removes a value nor reports inconsistency at any node of depth less than \(n\). If infeasibility can be certified only after rejecting every complete assignment, then the generated tree \(T_n\) is the full binary tree of depth \(n\). Consequently,
\[
\lvert T_n\rvert=\sum_{d=0}^{n}2^d=2^{n+1}-1,
\]
with \(2^n\) leaves. Under any computation model assigning \(\Omega(1)\) work to each visited node, the search therefore requires \(\Omega(2^n)\) time and \(\Theta(n)\) depth-first stack space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If propagation cannot prune or detect failure before all binary variables are assigned, exhaustive infeasibility certification visits 2^n leaves and requires exponential time.
knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Exponential Search Regimes
